speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DELIVERY OF RELIEF SUPPLIES TO BIAFRA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the past few days several questions have been asked of me in the House of Commons with respect to steps taken by the government of Canada to assist in the shipment of relief supplies to the civilian populations of the secessionist areas of Nigeria. Because it is desirable to set forth in a single statement the several aspects of Canadian efforts in this regard, the following brief chronological record has been prepared:
1.	In October 1968, Canadian Forces Hercules aircraft were despatched to the Nigerian area for use in carrying relief cargoes to Biafra. One of those aircraft joined the night airlift, the hazards and inefficiences of which were then and have always been recognized.
2.	In late October 1968, my personal representative, Professor Ivan Head, journeyed to Lagos for discussions with the Nigerian head of state, General Gowan, about the possibilities of additional relief shipments. It was as a result of that Canadian initiative that the Nigerians agreed to permit daylight relief flights subject to only a single condition, an undertaking by Colonel Ojukwu that he would not take advantage of the situation and fly in arms during daylight hours.

3.	The proposal for daylight flights on these terms was transmitted through the International Committee of the Red Cross and other channels to Colonel Ojukwu. When in November no reply had been received from Colonel Ojukwu, and the Nigerian government announced that it could no longer guarantee the safety of aircraft flying into Biafra at night, the Canadian government withdrew its aircraft. Canada stated at that time that it
would consider replacing the aircraft once appropriate daylight delivery arrangements were concluded.
4.	Not until June, 1969, some eight months following the announcement of the daylight relief flight proposal, did the Biafran authorities comment officially upon it. Not even then did Biafra accept the idea of daylight relief.. It only said that, subject to five conditions, it would be "willing to consider" daylight flights.
5.	Since early 1969, and with the knowledge of the Nigerian government, contacts have been made and discussions about relief and other measures subsequently held by Canada with representatives of the Biafran regime. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has spoken with Biafran authorities in New York; various Canadian officials have met with Biafran representatives in London, Ottawa, Geneva and New York, and are continuing to do so in one or more of these places whenever it appears appropriate to do so. It is in this light Mr. Speaker, that my statement of last week must be viewed when I said there had been contact at the ministerial level. This contact was made at New York; of course there have been other contacts at the official level in the various capitals, as I have just said.
6.	In an effort to overcome the delivery difficulties the Canadian government has consulted continuously with a number of other donor governments which make up what is known as the Hague Group. It has consulted as well with the United States government. That government, early this year, took the recognized lead in Nigerian relief activities when President Nixon appointed Ambassador Clyde Ferguson as his official representative to co-ordinate humanitarian assistance to Nigeria.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
7.	In June of this year I sent my representative back to Nigeria to ensure that General Gowon's single condition for daylight flights remained unchanged. Professor Head then journeyed to Tanzania on my behalf to speak to President Nyerere, the leader of an African country which had recognized the independence of Biafra, about all aspects of the Nigerian situation.

November 25, 1969
Minister's Statement on Biafran Relief
8.	On July 10, in an attempt to meet Biafran contentions that daylight flights would prejudice its military position, the Secretary of State for External Affairs offered to send Canadians to the area to act as inspectors of relief cargos.
9.	In the early summer the International Committee of the Red Cross began negotiations in Geneva in an attempt to solve the flight impasse which by then had reached a critical point as the Nigerian Air Force increased its efforts to prevent night flights of arms from reaching Uli. After one of its aircraft was shot down, the ICRC halted its night flights.
10.	A Red Cross proposal for daylight flights-I repeat, Mr. Speaker, this whole business of daylight flights was begun as a result of Canadian initiative-the whole idea was brought up as result of Canadian initiative which followed upon our obtaining from General Gowon his consent to such flights.

10. A Red Cross proposal for daylight flights was given to both Nigerian and Biafran representatives in Geneva on August 1. Biafra accepted the proposal in principle on August 14 but made its acceptance subject to the condition that it would continue to use Uli airport for its own operations. The Biafrans offered no evidence that

they were prepared to meet the single Nigerian request that arms not be flown in during daylight hours. The paper setting out "technical modalities" of daylight flights, drawn up by Professor Freymond of the ICRC and Dr. Cookey of Biafra, and circulated by the Biafran authorities, must be read in light of this Biafran condition.
11.	In late summer the ICRC sent a team of representatives to Nigeria in an attempt to conclude a daylight relief agreement with both sides, no agreement having been reached with either side up to this point. On September 13 the federal Nigerian government and the ICRC reached an agreement for an internationally-inspected and militarily-inviolable daylight relief airlift. The agreement included, at Nigerian insistence and reply to the Biafran condition for what amounted to daylight military use of Uli airport, a clause that the agreement should be without prejudice to military operations by the Nigerian government.
12.	The Biafran regime refused to conclude an agreement with the Red Cross. Biafra, instead, demanded in a press statement dated September 15 "a third party guarantee which will ensure that daylight flights are not used to military advantage by Nigeria." The statement continued to say that "the only guarantee acceptable to Biafra is that of a third government or international organization of a political character."
13.	The governments of Canada and the United States immediately attempted to provide assurances to meet this understandable Biafran fear of military disadvantage. Discussions toward this end took place in Ottawa and in Washington and involved officials of the Prime Minister's office and the Department of External Affairs and officials of the White House and the Department of State. Included in these discussions as one element of these assurances was a proposal for Canadian observers to travel on board relief aircraft.
14.	Canadian officials subsequently met with Biafran representatives in Geneva. Ambassador Ferguson, who had been agreed upon as the person who should convey formally these offers, travelled to Africa. As set forth in the Washington statement, dated November 12, 1969, the Biafran authorities on October 24 formally rejected the offers which were designed to protect Biafra from military disadvantage, which is exactly what they had asked for.
November 25, 1969

15.	Canadian officials in Geneva have been informed by Biafran representatives that Biafra demands more than military assurances; that, in addition, guarantees of a political nature are required in order to break the impasse. The Canadian government is not willing to give the political guarantees demanded as these would be tantamount to recognition of an independent state of Biafra, and an overt interference by Canada into the political affairs of another country, contrary to the resolutions of the Organization of African Unity.
16.	During the past several weeks, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has continued his discussions about Nigeria with some 25 other foreign ministers, many of them from African nations, at the United Nations. I talked to Secretary General U Thant about the problem in New York on November 11 as I had a year earlier. Canadian leaders have pursued the Nigerian issue with the leaders of two African countries who have visited Ottawa this fall. They were President Hamani Diori of Niger and President Nyerere of Tanzania. I can say that the unanimous view of these African leaders is that the Organization of African Unity resolutions must be respected.
17.	The government is now considering, as stated a few days ago, alternative means of delivering relief to Biafra in daylight. It does so while agreeing entirely with the recent statement of United States Secretary of State Rogers: "Daylight flights under agreed procedures . . . remain the only practicable scheme for an immediate and substantial expansion of relief operations."
18.	The government's concern remains, Mr. Speaker, as it has throughout, and as does that of hon. members opposite and indeed all Canadians, with the innocent civilian victims of this tragic war. Delivering adequate food and relief supplies to these people must be our resolve, notwithstanding the disinclination of the Ojukwu regime to accept it, except in return for political advantage.

Why has the government refused to assist Canairelief which has been and continues to transport substantial relief to the starving people of Biafra? Why, Mr. Speaker? Shortly after the Nixon administration took office and began to take some initiative in this area we pleaded with the government of Canada to support those measures but the government refused until November 12 when a statement was made by the United States Secretary of State, Mr. Rogers, which appeared to suggest that the United States government was backing away from the problem. Then the government of Canada courageously rushed to Washington's side.
I understand that about 1,500,000 people have starved since early in 1968 and that perhaps 2,000 a day are dying of starvation at this moment. Let us do what we can. Let the Prime Minister and his colleagues act to assist Canairelief in taking supplies to that country by night; let them provide this assistance rather than come to the House with a long statement designed to whitewash the whole picture and excuse the government of Canada from discharging its humane responsibility.

There is one thing in the statement which I am prepared to welcome: it is clear the right hon. gentleman is now aware of the great concern felt by the Canadian people about the immense human tragedy which has already cost between one million and two million

lives and which threatens to exterminate a whole people. What I find so regrettable about the lengthy and evasive statement we have heard is that there was no mention, as the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out, of the one thing, amid these different alternatives, which is staring the people of Canada in the face. The obvious place where our help should begin is in the operation which, despite danger and difficulties, is in fact being carried on by Joint Churchaid, to which Canairelief has given tremendous and heroic assistance.

Why is it that this channel of help is being neglected? It is suggested that Colonel Ojukwu should accept in their place daylight air relief flights. Is the Prime Minister aware-if he is, he has shown no sign of it-that the International Red Cross operation contemplates only the delivery of some 90 tons of supplies over a three week period under the control of the Nigerian army and air force authorities?
Canairelief is a voluntary organization. I should not say Canairelief because the organization also includes other voluntary bodies that have banded together in Churchaid, but the joint church operation is flying in 200 tons of supplies nightly. Is Colonel Ojukwu or anybody else being asked to accept a three weeks arrangement, tainted as it is, which would involve a much smaller amount of supplies? Is this going to help Colonel Ojukwu's own people? That is what the Prime Minister suggests. It is ridiculous to pretend that this operation cannot be assisted without causing some breach of protocol or improper intervention in the affairs of another nation. As a matter of international law the right of humane intervention has been recognized for centuries, and is still clearly attested to by recognized authorities in the field.
The most important factor of all has already been stated by the Leader of the Opposition, who pointed out that Canairelief operations have indirectly been supported to the tune of $800,000 by the United States government through payments to church agencies. The U.S. government can assist church agencies to do this job, and they are the only ones who are relieving starvation. Why cannot our government do the same thing? Earnest requests have been made by many Canadians to this effect.

There has been a long and elaborate discussion on the subject of daylight flights, and I noted certain significant omissions in the statement of the Prime Minister. He referred to a document that he did not admit was an agreement. Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that the only agreement was with Nigeria. I have in my hand what purports to be a copy of an agreement entered into by the Red Cross agency and the Biafran authorities on August 27, 1969, providing in detail for daylight flights. The statement, which is so loosely made, that Colonel Ojukwu has refused to allow daylight flights is not in accordance with the fact.
After this agreement was signed the Red Cross went to the federal Nigerian government and secured another agreement. What does this agreement provide? Paragraph 4 reads as follows:
Routings to and from Uli, call signs, radio communication, emblems, types of aircraft and flight schedules shall be as agreed from time to time by the ICRC with the Nigerian Air Force and the Nigerian Army.
Is it not perfectly clear that this is asking the Biafran authorities perhaps to sign their own death warrants? It is certainly asking them to surrender. What does the agreement go on to provide? The Prime Minister made something of the fact that Colonel Ojukwu was asking for certain military considerations in the proposals that he made. Paragraph 6.2 of this draft agreement between the International Red Cross and the Nigerian federal government provides:
This agreement shall be without prejudice to military operations by the federal military government.
Perhaps both sides are using propaganda in this battle, Mr. Speaker, and it is not surprising that they are. The Biafrans are fighting a war of survival and it would not be reasonable to expect them to agree to anything which might lead to their military defeat.
But there is more than just the propaganda of one side behind this matter. As long ago as last January General Alexander, a British member of the observer team in Nigeria, according to The Economist of January 11 spoke of a Nigerian plan, in collaboration with the British government, to propose certain relief measures which for military reasons would be unacceptable to the Biafran authorities, and which could then be used for propaganda purposes by blaming Colonel Ojukwu for Biafran starvation. This is precisely what has occurred. Indeed, when talking about propaganda it seems to me that the

In the name of humanity I implore the government to be big enough to look at this problem again. From time to time the government has stated that if its efforts to assist the International Red Cross are not successful, it will look at other avenues and approaches. Therefore let me end by urging the Prime Minister and the government to listen to what the Canadian people are saying, and to do something about helping the only agency that is relieving starvation in Biafra. The lives of hundreds of thousands depend on action of that sort, and there is no good reason for not taking it. I believe that the people of Canada demand that this action be taken.

Mr. Speaker, we have listened carefully to the 18-point statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) concerning the tragic situation in Nigeria and Biafra.
Mr. Speaker, this delicate, serious and very complex situation will not be solved by miracles, and the Prime Minister did not come up with a practical solution. In my opinion, he cannot make a miracle to set things right, not any more than the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who censures the government for its inaction but fails to recommend a concrete solution; or again, the NDP member who has just told us about the great human tragedy taking place in Biafra.
Mr. Speaker, we Creditistes are also members of the opposition and we sincerely believe that one of the 18 points expounded before the House is based nevertheless on actual facts and research. I say this not to flatter the Prime Minister or the government but out of respect for the truth.
Some Canadian officials went there, not to have a party, but to observe and study the situation. They met with representatives of both sides and even travelled to Great Britain to confer with Nigerian authorities. As for those Canadians, whoever they might be, who went to Nigeria, they have discussed the problems facing that country.
When either Nigeria or Biafra lays down conditions concerning relief to be sent by Canada, be it drugs, food, clothing, medical care, etc., it seems to me that we should in this House stop tearing one another to pieces,

DEBATES	November 25, 1989
as the Leader of the Opposition and the spokesman for the New Democratic party are doing at the present time.
We cannot always be at one another's throat and I shall speak straight out: if the Leader of the Opposition were in office instead of the present Prime Minister and told us what he would do in such circumstances, we would listen to him carefully.
Nobody wants more than we do to bring relief to those who are in distress- and are being massacred in Nigeria and in Biafra. But all the same, we must be realists and coldly look into the possibilities offered us to help them. We are asking the parties concerned to allow us to help them through the Red Cross, but they do not even want to hear of it. Are we to settle Biafra's future in the House of Commons of Canada? Let us be logical and consistent with ourselves. I hear the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) grumbling. This is all he can do in the House of Commons. Besides, he also does it outside.
No one here, except perhaps the hon. member for York South, can tell me that he is more anxious than we are to settle the dispute between Nigeria and Biafra. We want to help. However, as I said earlier, it is not by quarrelling with one another that we shall solve that problem.
Let us examine the solutions instead of saying simply to the Prime Minister: You are wrong, you have no solution to offer, you are arrogant toward Biafra, you do not want to commit yourself to supply assistance. I would like to know why logical, reasonable and truly human solutions are not suggested to the government to help parliament and the people of Canada to settle the disastrous situation prevailing in Nigeria and Biafra.
In our opinion, it is possible to work objectively if we offer solutions and ask for the assistance to those who are directly responsible. If the colonel of some country refuses to accept our aid and to co-operate, how can we undertake any action?
We are asked to intervene in the affairs of another country and to take position in favour of one side or the other from the political point of view. Mr. Speaker, if those leaders are out merely to save their political skins, it is time for the populations to find other leaders who can get along better with other heads of state.

A motion may, in case of urgent and pressing necessity previously explained by the mover, be made by unanimous consent of the House without notice having been given under Standing Order 42.
I shall heed your admonition of yesterday as to the brevity of one's explanation. In fact, I think no explanation of my motion is necessary at all. That the salary and indemnity of the Minister of Finance be reduced to $30 per week, and that he report to Parliament this day six months hence on whether it is possible for one person to live on this amount.

The House resumed from Monday, November 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gray that Bill C-140, to amend the Customs Tariff and to make a consequential amendment to the Excise Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, may I conclude the remarks I was addressing to the House last night. What I really wanted to say in the short time I have 
left is that, to put it in blunt words, in so far as the farmer and the people in Saskatchewan are concerned, the Kennedy Round has failed. The juggling of various tariff schedules as proposed in Bill C-140 will not, in the final analysis, mean anything to the people in Saskatchewan.
Previous speakers have outlined the facts of life as to how the tariff structure has affected the actual farmer on the land in Ontario and in Saskatchewan; but, if one wants to really look at some concrete examples, one can look at the development of the potash industry in Saskatchewan and the situation it is in now. Essentially, there is an impasse vis-a-vis Canadian and United States production. What the United States is saying, as a result of the congressional hearings held in Washington, is that first and foremost the jobs of the workers in New Mexico are going to be protected. Since this is their first consideration, it means that the ordinary process of negotiation, such as the Kennedy Round, will not protect the position of Canadian workers and it is probable that, despite the horrendous efforts of the Premier of Saskatchewan, negotiation will not protect the investment of Canadian companies in the potash industry in Canada. The moral of the lesson is that we have to look to the world markets if we are going to sell Canadian potash.
We are in a desperate position in the wheat economy, according to the papers that were presented to the Agricultural Outlook Conference in Ottawa yesterday and today. Mr. H. B. Huff, Assistant Professor of Agricultural Economics at the University of Guelph, speaking to the Conference, stated that policies are needed to stabilize prices and production, and to match production with demand. Dr. Huff described the dilemma of the wheat producers as "probably the most serious problem confronting Canadian agriculture".
I would go further than that and say that the wheat problem and the potash problem are two of the most serious confronting the total Canadian economy today. The juggling of the tariff schedules under the Kennedy Round will not offer a solution to either one of these problems. It is time the government of this country ceased proposing policies that were relevant to Canada in 1910 when Sir Wilfrid Laurier first looked at the agricultural economy in the west on behalf of a Liberal government. It is time this government realized it is 1969, not 1910. It is time they started to look at this economy in terms of how Canadians can live in the cut-throat economic jungle which exists in the world today.
November 25, 1969

What the people in Saskatchewan want to know is, how we are going to use the capital investment in the wheat industry and in the potash industry in Saskatchewan? How are we going to have sufficient jobs to maintain the population in that province? The answers will not be found in the tariff juggling that is proposed in Bill C-140.
If the government and this House doubt the seriousness of the situation, then they should certainly give consideration to a news report emanating from the convention of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. This press report in the Globe and Mail of November 25, 1969, reads as follows:
Western Canada should study the implications of secession if Ottawa does not give proper attention to western problems, the Saskatchewan wheat pool said yesterday. The comment was made in a statement released from the wheat pool's annual meeting and it did not elaborate.
The situation is serious when an organization as responsible as the Saskatchewan wheat pool issues such a statement from its annual meeting. The statement also indicated that, since farmers did not contribute to inflation they should not be affected by the budgetary restraints of the government. The meeting asked the federal government to subsidize interest rate charges over 7 per cent on farm improvement loans and to curtail high costs of farm production by the establishment of a prices and trade board.
Questions were repeatedly raised in this House today during the question period as to what was going to be done to stop escalating prices in this country. The people in the cities and on the farms in Saskatchewan are being crucified by the fiscal and trade policies that are being followed. I cannot over-emphasize the serious situation that exists. The government should give very careful consideration to the suggestions emanating from the Saskatchewan wheat pool convention with regard to interest rates and prices affecting farm production. Some steps should be taken to bring these important factors under control. Undoubtedly, this House will pass Bill C-140. What is implicit in that type of approach is that if we juggle the customs tariffs in Canada we will reach a state of competition which will result in a fair distribution of opportunity and earning power for the people who live, work and produce the wealth of this nation. It just has not happened, Mr. Speaker. The people who are in competition with one another are the farmers and the small businessmen, and these are the people who are

Customs Tariff-Excise Tax Act going broke in Canada today. It is not International Nickel, Imperial Oil, Gulf Oil or Shell Oil. The people who are going broke are those in competition with one another. I just cannot take seriously the exercise of juggling tariffs, Mr. Speaker, and I think it is only an exercise. It is not relevant to a good many people who live and work in this nation today.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on Bill C-140, my mind goes back over a number of years during which we on this side of the House have continually harangued and harped at the government to seriously consider the problems existing with regard to custom tariffs and excise duties, particularly as they apply to rural western Canada.
Bill C-140 brings up to date and ratifies the tariff schedules which have been in effect since June 3, 1968, as a result of the Kennedy Round tariff negotiations. What concerns me, Mr. Speaker, is that many of the items in tariff schedules approved by this House, such as the one we are now dealing with, are then left up to the officials to interpret, and more often than not the officials interpret them in the narrowest possible sense. They do not take into consideration the general theme or the intent of the legislation passed by Parliament. The government does not really give the intent of the legislation to the officials who have to police or interpret the act.
All across this country today we see groups of people rebelling against bureaucracy and the system; farmers in western Canada, university students and people in the cities trying to build homes. Why are they rebelling against the system? It is because the system is not paying any attention to the people of this country. The system does not give one particle of consideration to, their problem of staying alive and earning a fair standard of living. All across Canada, we see a certain amount of rebellion against the system because the bureaucracy built up by this and previous governments is finally reaching an unbearable stage for the people of this nation. I can quote many instances of this.
We see a great deal of apparatus and paraphernalia on which duties are being removed under Bill C-140. We also see some on which they are not being removed. I go back to the old complaint which I and other members raised in this House a number of years ago with regard to agricultural implements under tariff items 40924-1 or 40948-1. We come back to a long and detailed list of tariff
November 25. 1969

Customs Tariff-Excise Tax Act exemptions, and then a narrow interpretation placed on those tariff exemptions.
I will give some examples. In the tariff exemptions, sprinkler irrigation systems are duty-free. In another place, we find aluminum sluice-gate devices for the control of water in irrigation ditches. In another item we find that agricultural instruments and agricultural machinery might be duty-free, if not otherwise listed. It was pointed out very forcefully by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) that duty has to be paid on an irrigation pump which may or may not be used for a sprinkler system. Here, we see the very intent of the legislation and the whole tariff structure. The intent is to allow all agricultural machinery into Canada dutyfree, yet because one specific item is not spelled out, some narrow-minded official says, "Oh, oh, this wasn't the intent of the legislation". I argue it was the intent of the legislation because sprinkler irrigation systems are duty-free. Then, we have the example of sluice-gate pumps. Sprinkler irrigation systems and pumps are duty-free. In another item, we have aluminum pipe sluice-gate devices for the control of water in irrigation ditches.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
How much further must we go before we spell it out in complete detail? Then, at the bottom of the list, we find the words: "Agricultural implements or agricultural machinery and parts not otherwise listed." These are duty-free. Yet because officials are overconcerned with maintaining their own positions, we find them placing the narrowest possible interpretations on these items.
Last fall we experienced a difficult time in finding storage for damp grain. It became evident that silos could be used for this purpose.
I asked whether the minister would take the trouble to see whether silos could not come in duty-free. But there is no mention of this in Bill C-140. Action should have been taken. We find that the duty on ladders for silos is up 25 per cent; that steel wall sections, with or without doors, for the construction of steel silos attract rates of duty which have risen from 10 per cent to 25 per cent, and so on. Last year, when they faced this difficult storage position, many farmers resorted to the construction of steel or glass-lined silos and I maintain these items should be allowed to enter duty-free. After all, they are not made anywhere in Canada. Yet farmers have to pay duty at rates between 10 and 25 per cent because the government failed to act.

I submit that the total revenue flowing to the government from this source would amount to relatively little. Yet to the individual farmers concerned, this duty represents a considerable extra expense. To my regret, many farmers in parts of Saskatchewan, northern Manitoba and some parts of western Alberta along the foothills still face a situation in which many bushels of grain will have to be harvested damp. Silos could help meet this difficulty. In any case we could help farmers to diversify into a cattle feeding operation which would be of help to them in staying afloat during a risky period.
The government suggests that the federal sales tax on grain bins should be refunded to the purchasers. Yet I am informed by the department that the same consideration does not apply to Quonset buildings, since such buildings are not regarded as grain bins. A letter I have received says that a Quonset building may or may not be used to store grain; in other words, it may be used for some other purpose. Well, this enables the farmer to produce more efficiently. What I am complaining about is that we find no efficiency in government, no broadminded approach to the whole question of the application of the Customs Tariff and Excise Tax Act.
The whole principle of the bill we are considering involves a broader and more fair-minded approach to the application of the Acts to which I have just referred. Every member of this House should realize that this was the underlying purpose of the Kennedy Round negotiations. The intention was that the burden of customs and excise taxes should be reduced as far as possible. It is not difficult to pass legislation to confirm actions which have in fact been taken since June 3 of last year, but we ought not to do so without registering concern that the intent of the Kennedy Round is not being fully carried out by the officials working for the government. The minister responsible for piloting this measure through the House is a Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gray), with very little else to do. Surely, he could pursue this subject with the officials of his department to ensure that the full spirit and intent of the Kennedy Round negotiations is carried out by them. The time has come to take a close look at this whole field to determine whether we are treating all sections and minorities in this country fairly. It is not good enough for the government to have parliament pass pieces of legislation and then to pay no attention to the way in which sections of that legislation are applied.
November 25, 1969

This is one of the reasons which prompted me to speak on the particular bill before us. I want the government and the minister responsible for piloting this bill through the House to carry out the full intent of this legislation; that is to say, the most liberal interpretation of the Customs Tariff and of the Excise Tax Act. What I want to see is not a group of bureaucrats trying to enforce their will upon citizens who are trying to make a living but, rather, a group of officials who are trying to translate the intent of Parliament for the benefit of the people of Canada. When a situation of this kind is reached we shall find less and less evidence of anxiety among minorities, less and less evidence of anxiety in particular regions of this country. This is important to me, especially when one recalls the extract which the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) read from the Globe and Mail to the effect that the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, a conscientious, law-abiding, purely Canadian firm is suggesting that western Canada might secede if no attention is paid to prairie problems.
Canada, we cannot remind ourselves too often, consists of many regions spread across some 4,000 miles of territory. It is the home of many minorities. Surely, the government must be prepared to listen and respond to some of the wishes of these various regions and minorities if we are to stay together as a single, unified force.

Following that particular sitting of the House, I understand my hon. friend had a brief conversation with one of the officials, but as yet, perhaps as a result of an omission on my part or on somebody else's part- though I do not think that is directly relevant-it has not proved possible to arrange such meeting.
Let me repeat my invitation to the hon. member. I would be happy to convene such meeting, at which time we could review at greater depth than is possible in a forum of this kind the questions he has raised.
I might conclude my comment on this particular point by saying that Parliament has provided, in the passage of the legislation in question, procedures for those who are not satisfied with administrative rulings of officials. These rulings can be reviewed by the tariff board, and an appeal lies from the tariff board in certain cases to the Exchequer Court. This is the method provided by Parliament.
I recall my hon. friend referring yesterday to section 22 of the Financial Administration Act. I note that it is his intention to advise the people in his riding who may not be satisfied with administrative rulings to take advantage of this provision, by making application under it, and this is something they are fully entitled to do if they wish.
However, I might say that as far as I am aware there is nothing secret about this particular provision. It is part of a statute that has been passed by parliament. The statute appears in the Revised Statutes. If it is amended from time to time the amendments are printed in the annual statutes. These volumes are made available to all members of the House. If I am not mistaken, the Queen's Printer distributes them free to just about every public library and university library in Canada. So as I have said, there is nothing that is more secret about section 22 of the Financial Administration Act than any section in any other piece of legislation on the federal statute books. Certainly, my hon. friend is at liberty, as is any citizen of Canada, to see whether matters of concern to him qualify for consideration under the provisions of this particular statute.
While I understand the concern that he and other members have expressed about the manner in which they feel the officials seem to apply or to interpret various sections of the Customs Act, it seems to me that it is not the most helpful way to advance the consideration of these matters to attempt to suggest

Excise Tax Act that the attitude the officials are taking is founded on some type of ill-will or animus toward a particular group or section of the country.
Although officials are as capable as any other human beings of making mistakes from time to time, generally they try to carry out their duties in a way that they hope will be considered as being in the best interests of the public at large. As I have said, if my friend and I sit down together to review the administrative procedures, I do not say it will be immediately impossible to clear away the difficulties he so eloquently brought to the attention of the House, but at least it will help clarify matters and perhaps point the way to some solutions. Now that I have a somewhat greater responsibility for such matters I would be happy to try to assist hon. members and their constituents in obtaining fair and equitable treatment from the administration for their problems.

Mr. Chairman, I am not as learned in the law as my colleague the minister, and neither are the people I represent. I made no reference to anything that was secret. As I stated last night, my objection was that no effort was made by the bureaucrats to inform persons like myself, representing the farmers as I do, that there were other avenues we could pursue.
As far as the minister's comments today are concerned, let me remind him that although I outlined the problem to him last December he still has not fully understood it The department the minister represents, the Department of Finance, inserts these items in the schedules of the Customs Tariff. It is the duty of the officials of the Department of National Revenue, a different department entirely, to interpret these items. So although they are passed by Parliament, in effect they mean nothing.
The situation is this. One item in the schedule referred to "all other agricultural implements and all other agricultural machinery". That must mean something to those who inserted the item. Certainly, it meant something to the people of Canada, and particularly to the western farmers.
It now appears that the western farmers were under a misconception. They thought that all agricultural implements and agricultural machinery would be allowed into Canada duty free, something they were very happy about. Indeed, I think that was the intent of Parliament when this particular item was agreed to. However, over the years,

November 25, 1969
time and again the farmers have found that their interpretation was incorrect.
I remember spending three days with a constituent of mine trying to obtain an interpretation of this term which I have used so often. We both went to the officials of the Department of Finance, and they confirmed that this item was in the schedule. They said that nothing could be plainer, and we agreed. We then went to the Department of National Revenue and told them what the Department of Finance officials had said, to which the officials of the Department of National Revenue replied that it was they who were charged with the proper interpretation, which was different from ours.
This is the point that I have been endeavouring to clarify. Why is the item in the schedule if none of the officials know what it means? Why do not the Department of National Revenue officials tell the Department of Finance to spell out the meaning of the item? We who represent the farmers are not legal minded, but the language used is plain enough to us: an agricultural implement is an agricultural implement, one that can be used for the production of agricultural products.
The contention of some of these very narrow-minded officials is that any agricultural implement that can be used for some purpose other than agriculture is no longer an agricultural implement. I say this is foolish, because every implement used on the farm can be used for some other purpose. If that interpretation were correct, there would be no such thing as an agricultural implement or an agricultural machine; so let us strike out these words and we will know where we are.
I have discussed this matter with both the minister and his officials. Last December 3 the minister was under the impression that all agricultural implements and machinery were allowed into Canada duty free; as far as he was concerned there were no ifs, ands or buts. He interpreted the item to mean what it says, as I suggest the officials should unless there is good reason not to.

that Bill C-155, to amend the Excise Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a committee of the whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief remarks to explain and describe the nature of the measure before us. This bill is intended to implement the proposal in the budget speech of June 3, 1969, that a tax be imposed on the price of tickets or other charges for carrying passengers by air. As explained by the Minister of Finance at that time, the cost of construction and maintenance of air transportation facilities is very high and, in addition to obtaining revenue from user charges at airports, the government has decided that it is advisable to ask parliament to require individuals who travel by air to pay an amount through what, in effect, will
Excise Tax Act
be a special tax to help defray the costs of providing air transportation facilities.
When the proposed tax on tickets or other charges for transporting passengers by air was announced during the June 3 budget statement, the Minister of Finance said:
We shall wish to consult with the air carriers about detailed problems of defining and administering a measure of this kind.
Therefore, during the preparation of this bill a number of meetings took place between air carriers, their associations and government officials. These meetings were extremely helpful and the bill now before the House reflects a great many of the proposals and suggestions of the carriers concerning the application and administration of the proposed tax.
In devising a tax on tickets and other charges with respect to transporting passengers by air, it was necessary to recognize that the air transportation business, perhaps more than any other, operates across international boundaries on a world wide basis. In many cases, passengers have a free choice between travel on Canadian carriers or those of other countries. It was also necessary to keep in mind that the United States imposes an ad valorem tax on air transportation at the rate of 5 per cent but that it does not at present impose a tax on international air transportation except for flights into Canada and Mexico.
The proposed tax would be what is known as a consumption tax. In other words, it would be imposed on purchases by people in Canada of air transportation. The proposed tax will be in two forms. It will be an ad valorem tax at the rate of 5 per cent on the amount paid for transportation, in certain cases, and a flat dollar amount in certain other cases. The tax, whether ad valorem or flat amount, will be paid at the time when the purchaser of transportation buys a ticket. It would not, therefore, be a departure tax or airport tax to be collected at airports. The 5 per cent ad valorem tax will apply to tickets purchased in Canada for transportation within Canada, to the United States, and to the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The flat tax will be a tax of $5 but it may be reduced by Order in Council to an amount of not less than $2. It would apply to overseas flights where tickets are purchased in Canada

November 25, 1969
Excise Tax Act
for transportation that begins at a point in the taxation area and ends at a point ouside the taxation area. The term "taxation area" is more fully defined, as hon. members will note, in the bill before us. Where an amount is paid for the charter of an aircraft the 5 per cent tax, if applicable, will be on the amount paid by the person or group for the charter of the aircraft and not on the amount paid by each passenger. The flat tax, if applicable, will be calculated on the number of seats in the aircraft. The tax, whether ad valorem or a flat amount, will apply on charter flights that depart from Canada, even if the contract for the charter or the amount for transportation is paid outside Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say I will be pleased to attempt to answer more detailed questions that hon. members may have when the bill is in committee. I, therefore, ask the House to support the measure at the second reading stage.

At
the outset, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say we of the official opposition support the principle that those who use the services should be expected to pay for them. However, I do not say that without some qualifications. I wish to point out the principle used by the government in drawing up this bill leaves a great deal to be desired. What is being done is an attempt to recover a basic amount for the provision of certain services by the government of Canada with regard to airports.
The first point I wish to make is that this service varies from one city to another. Regardless of where persons fly from or what their destination is in Canada, they will have to pay on the same basis. Secondly, having an ad valorem tax on tickets again raises a point about which I was complaining during the discussion of the previous bill. The one who is going to have to pay the most is the person who flies the farthest; in other words, the people living at the extremities of the country.
A person living in Edmonton or Calgary will have to pay $10, give or take a few cents, on a ticket to Toronto or Ottawa. During that flight the passenger will use two airports, the point of departure and the point of arrival. A person flying from Toronto to Windsor or London, Ontario, will pay a much lesser amount. In fact, a passenger flying from Toronto to Ottawa on a round trip ticket will pay approximately $1.90 ad valorem. If my

memory serves me right, the round trip costs $38, giving a $1.90 ad valorem.
The rate is $42.

I stand corrected. It would then be $2.10 ad valorem. That passenger would also use two airports, Toronto and Ottawa. The passenger coming from Edmonton or Calgary to Toronto has paid approximately five times as much, but has not used any more facilities. I do not think he has to pay $8 for the communications network, therefore I do not see the reason for this ad valorem tax.
In addition, there are vast areas in this country, such as in the north, where the only means of communication is by air travel. One need only study the schedules of the airlines flying out of Edmonton, Prince Albert or Winnipeg to see the cost of the fares. Fine print in this context means type smaller than the main body of the print in the contract. The entire aim is to protect the consumer.

November 25, 1969
Criminal Code

I shall not deal with the aspect of the proposal which has already been pointed out by hon. members on this side to the effect that this is a provincial matter. The hon. member admits that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has been saddled with the responsibility of fighting such abuses as he describes. This is not merely a matter of the size of the print. Anyone who suggests that the civil law does not cover this point has simply not studied the law. The hon. member may be surprised to learn that the civil courts have been well ahead of him for 20 years. Anyone who has practised law or who has talked with lawyers would find that the size of the print does not matter at all. If a judge or a civil jury finds that the purpose of anything in a contract, or, possibly, even a parking ticket, is to keep the plaintiff, or the person directly concerned, uninformed, or to defeat the purpose of the contract, or to defraud the person concerned, the fact that it is included in the contract would have no bearing at all on the case. The common law
November 25, 1969

has given credence to exactly what the hon. member now tries to achieve by using the criminal law. I dare the hon. member to give me one case during the last five years where the argument that the inclusion of a fine print clause was meant to hide something, and was given credence by the court, was not thrown out as a defence to the action. I suggest to the hon. member that his bill is a repetition of the existing law.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The nature of man being what it is, it does not seem to matter whether the print is large or small. A few years ago I recall the government of Ontario passing a law that provided that all automobiles sold in Ontario as used cars must bear a certificate stating in half inch block letters whether or not the car was roadworthy. In effect, every car that was from then on sold in Ontario was represented in large block letters as being unroadworthy, yet people bought the cars just the same. I have not seen one certificate in the last four years declaring that a car was roadworthy. This law was ignored until the passage recently of provincial legislation respecting dealerships, which are now compelled to make their cars roadworthy before sale. So, surely the size of the fine print is not the criterion for judging whether we should include the matter within the criminal law, as suggested by the hon. member.
Is it not strange that he and his party have declared that the criminal law must not be applied to those who smash windows, set buildings on fire and use violence, because these people are reformers? Yet today, we see not only the hon. gentleman opposite but also many Canadians declaring that the protection of property does not necessarily involve criminal jurisdiction; that a person who damages property, or even threatens the life and limb of others in the cause of rebellion, should not be judged according to our criminal law. They also declare that use of drugs should not be a criminal matter.
The hon. member is saying, in effect, that those who throw Molotov cocktails while parading in Montreal, Vancouver, or on university campuses should not be charged with criminal offences because they are acting in the cause of rebellion. Yet someone who prints a contract containing a clause in fine print may, if the hon. member's bill passes, be sent to jail for three months. The hon. member cannot have it both ways. I am not suggesting for one moment that in protecting 21545-7
Criminal Code
private property one is justified in committing assault; whether the theft of private property is punishable by imprisonment is something for the court to decide.
I suggest this bill would further restrict the provisions of the Criminal Code. Today, we can be sent to prison for refusing to take a breathalyzer test. There are also provisions relating to impaired driving, but I do not drive. Although the Criminal Code is embracing new concepts, at the same time I feel we are restricting it. If the hon. member's bill were adopted, then what about such matters as riding a bicycle on the wrong side of the road?
With regard to false and misleading advertising, the question of what is false and misleading has not yet been decided. If someone were to sell me a product which he claimed was the best available on the market, and a month later I found one that was better, would this person go to jail? Of course not.
Not only would the incorporation of this provision into our criminal legislation be reversing the trend today; this matter is already being taken care of by other government departments. We are all aware that some people continue to promote ideas even though the world has passed them by. I am reminded of those young "Turks" who 35 years ago were disciples of John Maynard Keynes. Today these disciples are in power and are plugging the concepts of Keynes for all they are worth. The fact that they have no relevance to today's society does not faze them. Neither is the hon. member fazed by the fact that he is proposing a measure that he admits does not come within federal jurisdiction. As I say, the point is already covered by the common law.

As the representative in the House of a part of the population, I think the matter to be debated has two sides, as do most of the problems submitted to us.
On the one hand, I cannot help but congratulate very warmly the sponsor of the bill which aims primarily at protecting the Canadian consumer, since particularly in the last few years, we have paid attention to the problem.
That aspect of commercial, insurance and loan companies contrac.s is the one that should be examined by the government and more especially by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford). Indeed, I also feel that the form of those contracts raises every day some problems for the purchaser or the policy-holder.
It is often stated that those who buy insurance do not take the time to get acquainted with the terms of their contract. The reason is that those contracts are quite elaborate and that certain clauses appear in fine print. If such contracts were drafted in a plainer and clearer style, they would contribute to protect the ci izens.
On the other hand, I notice that the hon. member has introduced this bill several times in recent years and I have the impression that he always does it in the same way.
A moment ago I was reading the speeches made last February in connection with this bill and I realize that the member is again introducing his bill in the same way, supporting it whh nearly identical arguments except that he acknowledges the provincial jurisdiction and the part played in this field by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
The hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) could have given more de ails on the nature of discrepancies or other weaknesses inherent in these con'racts. He should have given examples and been more explicit as this would have made it easier for us to offer sound criticism.
The government has a part to play as regards the protection of the public in most cases where goods and services are bought. I feel that if we study existing legislation, whether provincial or federal, we realize that certain laws contain provisions to protect the public in this matter.
Perhaps the member goes too far in always presenting his bill the same way. The creation of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs seems to be a striking example of

the fact that mostly in the last few years the government has developed an increasing awareness of its responsibilities which it is ready to assume fully.
Does the problem come solely under federal jurisdiction? Although I am certainly not competent to express an opinion in this regard, it is my modest personal view that the provinces, even if they do not have a strong say in the matter, should at least assume responsibility for providing legislation to solve problems which might arise in this area.
I believe all the provinces of Canada have adopted such laws.
However, I also know that several professional groups in Canada have formed associations, not for the protection of their members, but primarily to protect the public against poten ial abuse on the part of members of associations or corporations.
Moreover, I know that insurance agents throughout Canada have joined professional associa dons and that insurance companies, as well as insurance agents both individually and in small groups are increasingly making continued and serious efforts in order to improve the general skill of their members so as to serve the public better.
It is a fact that, in Canada, the federal government, the provincial governments and several associations are on the lookout for those problems and keep a con.inuous watch so as to protect the public.
It also seems that if Canadians wish, for instance, to buy insurance policies or to benefit from advantages offered by finance companies or others, they can get informa.ion on what they buy and on what they are getting into through the news media, namely TV, newspapers and advertising handouts, which are becoming more efficient every day. I have in mind here a certain kind of advertising finance companies usually go for.
Further more, every year, in each region, the agent who has sold more than a million dollars' worth of insurance receives some kind of honour. In my opinion, besides stimulating the agent who earns his living by doing adver ising insurance companies, that indirectly makes the public aware that such an agent is trustworthy because many citizens relied on him during the year by passing on to him their insurance problems.

I am no lawyer, but nevertheless, when I see the ways of our society, I find that the

citizen is protected by provincial laws in this respect and that he can also resort to civil courts. Lawyers claim it is easier to resort to civil courts than to criminal ones in that connection.
I was saying at the beginning of my remarks that both sides of the medal had to be considered. Indeed, we all are in favour of protecting the consumer and we all wish for serious steps to be taken for that purpose. For some time, in various places and in government circles, people have been talking about protecting the consumer and putting a ceiling on prices and wages. printed contract under conditions laid down by the Civil Code.

-Everyone who, with intent to mislead-

If the hon. member for Surrey really wants to help the public, he should eliminate, as far as he can, the possibilities of legal proceedings.

As for insurance companies, the clauses of their contracts should be more explicit. To show that such contracts are very difficult to understand, I shall take the liberty to read the statutory conditions related to fire insurance in the province of Quebec, and I quote section 16:
Should any disagreement arise as to the value of the insured property, of the property saved or as to the amount of the loss, such value or amount and the proportion (if any) that the company will have to disburse shall be submitted (whether the right to recover under the policy is discussed or not, and independently from all other questions) to the arbitration of a person chosen by both parties, or, if they cannot come to an agreement, then to the arbitration of three persons, one to be chosen by the insured, another by the company and the third by the first two persons chosen or, if they cannot come to an agreement, by a judge of the Superior Court sitting in the district where the loss happened; and such arbitration is subject to the provisions of article 1431 and following article of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Speaker, I do not understand any of this. I am a licenced insurance agent and even if I tried to explain it to a client, I would not succeed. Even if it were written in large print, such as is used on the first page of a policy, I think it would not be any easier to explain.
The hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) should, through his bill, ensure that such contracts are more precise.

November 25, 1969
Criminal Code
I believe that contract clauses should not come under the Criminal Code, because, generally, they are signed by two willing parties who are aware of the commitments they are making.

speakeroldname: Mr. Yves Forest (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FINE PRINT CLAUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I am to congratulate the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) for introducing this bill, I do so mainly because of his patience and perseverance, for this bill was not passed by hon. members when it came before the House in 1967 and 1969. Hon. members were right in so doing, as it seems evident that this bill to amend the Criminal Code deals mainly with a provincial and civil law matter.
However, the hon. member's objectives certainly are very praiseworthy, for if this bill succeeds in calling public attention to the danger of signing contracts whose meaning one understands only when they have been signed, the bill will have achieved, together with the relevant discussion, a useful purpose.
The hon. member likely wants to draw attention of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to the need to warn the public against this danger.
The explanatory notes say that insurance companies should be prohibited from embodying in their contracts fine print clauses. I think the problem is real, even if the hon. member never mentioned specific cases. As a matter of fact, I have often noted that people almost never read contracts, and even less insurance policies. Even the clauses printed in large characters are difficult to understand, except for lawyers specializing in this field. Other people rely on the salesmen to explain to them the terms of the contract.
The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) is nodding his agreement. He sells insurance and he knows what I mean.
Whenever a disaster or an accident occurs, people wake up; they try to understand what is happening and get in touch with their insurance broker or their lawyer.
I believe that the goal being sought by my hon. friend is indeed commendable, but that the bill itself is rather inadequate, especially as concerns amending the Criminal Code. Let

us refer to the terms used in section 328A to be inserted.
Sub-clause (2) reads as follows:
-the expression "small typographical character" means a typographical character that is substantially smaller than the one used in the body of the printed matter of the document.
I find this somewhat vague. What would happen, for instance, if the whole contract were printed in such typographical characters? The said section would then have very little meaning.
I would prefer the suggestion of the hon. member. The essential clauses in insurance policies, intended to exclude the liability, should be printed in different characters and in red in order to call the attention of the contracting parties, because as a rule they are not included in the statutory terms of insurance policies. Certain clauses are particularly important for the insured or for a party to a contract of another nature, whether it be an instalment or financing contract. In fact, the citizens do not realize, for instance, that they have one year only to file a claim and that they have barely a few weeks to produce a proof under oath in support of a claim. Failure to meet these conditions might cause the insured to lose some of his rights. Therefore, it would be important if for instance one could easily take note of these conditions.
They should be underlined or printed in another colour in order to call the attention of the contracting parties because, although they might consult a lawyer or an insurance broker, the time for their appeal might have lapsed. This suggestion could be usefully considered if we wish to protect the consumers and the insured public.
The bill deals with an indictable offence. That might be going a little too far. If we had really wanted to amend the Criminal Code, it might have been better to make it an offence punishable on summary conviction, since the penalty provided in this case does not seem as severe as that provided for an offence punishable on summary conviction. Furthermore, the bill says and I quote:
Everyone who, with intent to mislead, prints or causes to print in small typographical character.
Therefore, the offence would lie in the fact that someone prints or causes to print something. I cannot understand how this is an offence. The offence would rather consist in distributing or selling any article under a contract written in fine print.
November 25, 1969

Where deceit is the obvious purpose, we must not forget that the Criminal Code provides for the real cases of fraud, and legal action can be taken against the person who, in a deliberate attempt to deceive would have made people buy, for instance, an article under false representations. This happens often but does not apply so much to insurance contracts which, in general, are pretty standard and in which there is no false representations. This applies especially to the contracts used by canvassers who sell articles under false representations and who make people buy lots in Florida, sewing machines or family trees. They often tell people that they are not really buying anything, that they are not committing themselves to anything, while the latter end up by signing a contract, probably with full knowledge of the facts.
The Criminal Code and even the Civil Code provide for the annulment of a contract in case of fraud.
But the main objection to the bill is that its purpose falls within provincial jurisdiction. It therefore behoves the provincial authorities to pass legislation to protect those who sign such contracts and to set the rules governing all contracts, but more particularly insurance contracts. Insurance companies are members of responsible associations such as the Federation of insurance agents and insurance companies. There are also insurance superintendents. Most of the provinces have adopted laws and regulations on insurance. To my mind, and generally speaking, the public is well enough protected in that field.
The legislative assemblies are authorized to legislate on this matter. I maintain that the hon. member did well to draw those cases to the attention of the public. Indeed, he has done useful work and we trust that the people will be grateful to him for it But, though he is entitled to our congratulations, I do not feel that we can adopt this bill or refer it to a committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the arguments put forward by my colleagues and I would merely like to endorse a few of them.
People who intend to mislead may do so whether the print used is large or small.
However, I can understand that the consumer's first reaction may be to resort to such an excuse when he has been fooled, as we say. The first excuse that comes to his mind is that he had not read the contract. Even if the
Criminal Code
contract had been read and re-read to him, he will always resort to the same excuse. The one who was fooled by some contract always claims that the clauses were in very fine print and that he signed it without question because the print was too small to be read.
I do not believe we could do away with fraud by passing this bill. That is why I found sensible the argument put forward by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin), namely that the size of the print does not matter, what matters is that one should understand the clauses of a contract. That is the point to be considered, for whenever a person feels wronged by the terms of a duly signed contract, it is not because of the fine print of the clauses but because the wording was incomprehensible or ambiguous, since anyone could give it any meaning he wished.
It is through the purposely unintelligible wording of contracts that people are misled and not because of the size of the print. This, however, is quite likely to happen, and some take advantage of the small print to insert clauses which are not to the advantages of the customer.
When we deal with such matters, we must protect the customer by looking more fully into the problems and by finding ways of detecting real fraud. People claim they are fooled because of the fine print as a pretext for refusing to sign a contract. In some cases, the fact that fine print is used does indeed protect the people who then use it as a pretext.
I am far from denying the merits of the bill introduced by the hon. member. Of course, we all want to protect the consumer. But that is not the real problem, and whether there is a problem or not, it is up to the provincial governments to solve them.
