Mr. Warren Allmand (Noire-Dame-de-
Grace): Mr. Speaker, while I fully support the principles which prompted the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) to introduce this bill, I do not think the bill properly deals with the problem. As a matter of fact, I think it is a bad bill because the fine is not large enough. Under this bill a man could be in the class of which the hon. member complains, pay the fine or undergo the penalty and still make a great deal of money. This is a very important problem and one with which I have dealt

November 25, 1969
Excise Tax Act
many times in my practice as a lawyer in cases where people were duped by big business because of clauses in contracts; and not only big business, but firms like jewellers, dry cleaners, etc. I acted in a case concerning a ski-tow that involved many thousands of dollars. It was written on the tow ticket that all fault and responsibility was excluded. A young boy went on the ski-tow and was injured, fracturing his skull, his back and many other parts of his body. The company tried to get out of its responsibility because it was written on the ticket, which is a contract, in big print that they would not be responsible.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this type of bill will not meet the problem. We need to bar any exclusion of responsibility in written contracts, whether they are big or small. I do not think that anybody in business should be able to make a profit out of exclusion from fault or responsibility. I do not think this bill covers the problem. It is true that in the courts of some provinces this type of clause excluding responsibility or fault has been outlawed, but they have not gone far enough.
I think that if the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) proceeds with the policy he has enunciated, it will fill the gap. There are those who argue against this proposition and cite the principle of caveat emptor, "Let the buyer beware", stating that when a man enters into any kind of agreement or contract he should realize what he is doing and bear full responsibility for it. We know that the services and goods sold on the market today are so technical and so complex-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FINE PRINT CLAUSES
speechtext:
Order, please. The hour appointed for the consideration of private members' business having expired, I do now leave the chair. The House will resume at 8 p.m.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Gray (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-155, to amend the Excise 
Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, at the five o'clock adjournment I had discussed in part those aspects of the principle of the bill that I wish to cover at this stage of the debate. I emphasize once more that the opposition has no basic objection to having the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) recover some of the costs of operating Department of Transport airports and related services from persons using those services and airports. However, I had indicated my objection to the principle of an ad valorem tax on tickets which is based on the quantum of the ticket. This principle will throw a disproportionate burden on those persons who are flying long distances and it will adversely affect the sparsely settled areas of the country, particularly the north and the mountain areas where a good deal of flying is done but at high cost. Minimal facilities are provided there by the Department of Transport.
Therefore, I would feel it preferable to collect a flat rate from every passenger, as is done at many airports in foreign countries. As a matter of fact, that is what is proposed to be done with regard to passengers leaving on flights overseas. I think it would be much simpler if there were an agreed charge: While some people might object that those on relatively short flights are paying a higher incidence of tax than those on longer flights, it seems to me that the same revenue would accrue to the government from an average and fairly minimal charge. I do not know what the experience will be as to what should be the average charge, but I am sure it will not be disproportionate to the 5 per cent charge to the great bulk of passengers who fly on shorter, commuter routes in Canada.
Having examined the bill, I feel that the government is imposing on business and industry the entire cost of collecting this tax. To my mind the airline companies, particularly the smaller ones, will have the burden imposed on them of collecting and remitting the tax. If you look at the bill itself, Mr. Speaker, you will find that quite a burden is imposed upon every airline that will be subject to the tax. I say airline, but some of them will be merely air services.
On examining the bill, you will see that a licensed air carrier has the duty of collecting the tax which is a debt to Her Majesty. There must be a monthly return in respect of taxes. In fact, there must be a nil return in those cases where services which are operating in
November 25, 1969

the much more thinly populated regions of the country cannot, between seasons, carry any passengers; they have to file a nil return. There are severe penalties for default. I am sure that if I were to examine all the fine print in the bill and read all the regulations it is proposed to pass, I would discover that a trust will be imposed on the moneys in the hands of the licensed carrier. These moneys are collected on behalf of Her Majesty. Therefore, they fall into the same category as all other forms of taxes that are collected and receive a certain priority.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the government could quite easily make some adjustment based upon the quantum of taxes being remitted, in order to pay for these services. This tax money will amount to quite a large amount. But here we go again: the government wants money and it is telling the businessmen involved, "You are going to pay for the cost of collecting this tax." I think it is about time the government paid to have these taxes collected. We find that in the bill this is the businessman's responsibility. I submit that it is the responsibility of the government and is not the responsibility of the businessmen concerned. I hope there will be some changes in this regard.
I think other members of the opposition wish to make remarks on this bill, and I am sure some government backbenchers will wish to speak to it. I invite comments from hon. members such as the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange) and those representing the developing regions of Quebec and Ontario. I think we all wish to see how they react to this 5 per cent surcharge on almost the only, and very essential, form of transportation in their constituencies, transportation which covers not only business but pleasure and the development of their areas. If they think this is a fair impost, I should like to hear them say so, in order that their constituents may consider the position of those hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, it has been my experience that one can criticize the Liberal Party in almost any way as long as you give its members credit for being businesslike. If there is anything this government is proud about, it is that it runs a businesslike operation. The Liberals think they know how to run the country. Mr. Speaker, I suggest in very mild terms that they are disastrous as businessmen. All the time they feed us with phony propositions, as
Excise Tax Act
if we cannot see through them. This bill is another of those propositions.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Who is going to be paying this tax? Let us face up to the situation. The government starts by saying that some of the deficits in operating airports have to be recovered. I believe the deficit is in the neighbourhood of $57 million. This proposal, if passed, will bring in another $20 million and will still leave a deficit of $37 million on the operation. It has been in the past, and will continue to be, a subsidy to business. It has always been of this nature and no one is really taking any exception to this.
When this government hands out some old age pensions it thinks it is doing a great job, but it does it in a very meagre way. The government says, "We are subsidizing the poor, and we should not do so much subsidizing". But when the government subsidizes the rich, it does not count for much. This situation has been continuing for a long time and will go on even after this legislation is passed, if it is the disposition of the House to pass it.
The only people who will pay this 5 per cent tax are those in groups which charter flights, because that form of air travel is all they can really afford. I have experience of many of these groups. They consist of people who have saved for years in order to get back to the old country and visit their relatives and friends. They travel on these flights because of their relatively low cost. These are the people who will pay more. There is no way they can pass off this 5 per cent tax, just as there is no way they can pass off the airline ticket. That is part of the double standard of taxation in Canada.
What difference does it make to the businessman if we add another 5 per cent to his airline ticket? The whole amount was deductible before, and it will still be deductible. The government will be paying part of those costs. If it is not the government which pays, the additional tax will be reflected in higher prices being charged by the company concerned. The same pretence is being made here, namely, that we are trying to put airport operations on a paying basis. In fact, the subsidy is simply being transferred from one point where it is very visible to another point where it is not so visible, because of our tax system.
This is not the only thing the tax system conceals, but it is an example of how these

November 25, 1969
Excise Tax Act
things get swallowed up in a tax system. The government will either lose revenue or prices will rise to take care of this situation. This is a sort of peanuts operation the government is running. What is particularly infuriating is that there was an opportunity in the past -and the opportunity still exists-for the government to recover large sums of money which could have been applied against the operating losses of airports. I am referring to the fact that we started off in Canada with a solitary airline, Air Canada. The minute it started to do well, the government introduced a competitor. Every time they appear to be doing fairly well, the government makes certain there is a competitor to interfere with its operation. We in this party believe it is far more effective and businesslike to run airlines on an efficient, profitable basis rather than embarking upon the kind of taxation gerrymandering that is being suggested in this piece of legislation.
We in this party believe that the government has an obligation to state clearly its policy with respect to Air Canada and to end the uncertainty and speculation that has placed a cloud on the future of Air Canada. The impression persists that the Liberal government, with its usual concern for the interest of big business, is preparing to hand over all or part of Air Canada to private ownership. The chairman of Air Canada, appointed by this government, began his term of office in January by openly advocating the merger of Air Canada with Canadian Pacific Airlines. Had he suggested we take over Canadian Pacific Airlines, as we should, that would have been something else. They never should have been allowed in the field. The idea of a merger will not appeal to the taxpayers of this country. The week after that statement was made, Canadian Pacific was authorized to increase its transcontinental service from two daily flights in each direction to five, perhaps the most ill-timed administrative decision in Canadian history.
One would assume that if a merger was really under consideration, the government would do nothing in the interval to strengthen the hand of Canadian Pacific. Instead, the government and the Canadian Transport Commission, headed by a former Liberal minister of transport, have placed Canadian Pacific in a position in which to demand a larger share of the ownership and control of the merged airline in the event that a merger takes place. We cannot help viewing these events in light of the fact that the Minister without Portfolio from Manitoba (Mr. 
Richardson), who has been placed in charge of air transport policy by this government, until recently was a director of Canadian Pacific and a major holder of its common stock.
We do not dispute Mr. Pratte's claim that money would be saved by having a single transcontinental and international airline. Unlike the Liberals, we have consistently adhered to that posiiion. We have also insisted that that airline remain under public ownership. Since the public pays for the construction of airports and in effect subsidizes the whole industry, private entrepreneurs must not be allowed to reap a major share of the profits. We know that in a thinly populated country it makes no sense to have two airlines trying to duplicate one another's schedules, particularly when Air Canada will within two years be operating aircraft which have twice the seating capacity of those now in service. Duplication of service reduces load factors and increases costs, and we note with concern that the major airlines are rumoured to be considering another increase in domestic fares. On top of that there will be this additional 5 per cent tax.
On the other hand, we must point out that the uneconomic situation which exists did not arise mysteriously from natural causes; it is the result of deliberate government policy over a period of more than 20 years. Under both Liberal and Conservative governments the only consistent principle behind our air transport policy seems to have been concern for the interests of Canadian Pacific. The unstated assumption has been that Canadian Pacific has a natural right to as large a share of the air transportation market as can be given to it, at Air Canada's expense, without placing Air Canada in an over-all deficit position.
Canadian Pacific became an international airline because of the decision of a Liberal government in 1948. That decision, which reversed Mackenzie King's policy of keeping international air routes in public hands, was announced a few days after Parliament had adjourned-and nothing seems to have changed since then-so that the government could avoid parliamentary criticism of its actions. In his comparative study of the relations between governments and airlines David Corbett, an Australian political scientist, notes that this decision "marked the declining influence of Mackenzie King in the Liberal cabinet as his retirement approached in 1948, and
November 25, 1969

the rising power of the friends of the businessman in the Liberal Party". That power continued to rise in the following years and Canadian Pacific was permitted to extend its routes from the Pacific to Europe and Latin America. Canadian Pacific became a transcontinental airline as a result of a decision made and announced by the Conservative government during the 1958 election campaign.

Thank
goodness it was.

Well, now you will be paying an extra 5 per cent. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is arguing against the necessity of imposing a 5 per cent increase to defray the cost of airports. We could have had this as profit from Air Canada had we not introduced unnecessary competition.

sit in a comfortable pew.

Although the decision was arrived at in principle before any study of its economic implications could be made, the government commissioned Mr. Wheatcroft to prepare the first of his famous reports on airline competition in Canada. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), who was then minister of transport, told Mr. Wheatcroft that in his view "The time has come for the introduction of some measure of competition on our transcontinental routes".

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I must say I am having some difficulty relating his remarks to the bill before the House. As I understand it, the bill is designed to amend the Excise Tax Act. As the hon. member knows, I am prepared in all these matters to give him the benefit of the doubt, but it does seem the remarks he has been delivering go well beyond the scope of this bill and deal with a matter which is quite extraneous to the bill.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)

With the greatest respect, Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out that we are opposing the present tax measure. We are suggesting an alternative to the present proposal and we are trying to support our position which is, simply, that if there was one public carrier in Canada, that carrier would be more profitable and this country
Excise Tax Act
would be able to save the 5 per cent tax now proposed. I hope, Mr. Speaker, you appreciate my position; I have to outline the way in which I believe this could come about. The Wheatcroft report discovered, however, that exposing the publicly-owned airline to transcontinental competition would wipe out the profits on that service needed to cover the losses on its other domestic services. This situation was not expected to change for several years.
In January, 1959, the minister announced his acceptance of a recommendation by the Air Transport Board that CPA be allowed to operate one daily transcontinental flight. In this curious recommendation the board found that additional transcontinental air services would have a major detrimental effect on existing operations, but overruled its own conclusions on the peculiar grounds that Canadian Pacific's position as an international air carrier needed strengthening. The transcontinental flight was supposed to serve this purpose by connecting its existing international operations.
The inauguration of the CPA service diverted traffic from the publicly-owned airline without increasing the total volume of traffic, and contributed to massive deficits suffered by both airlines over the next few years. In 1960 even the Liberal members of this House voted to condemn the government for unnecessary duplication of domestic transcontinental airline services which denied TCA the opportunity to implement a further reduction in fares. But once they returned to office in 1963 the Liberals reverted to old habits.
Rumours of an impending merger between the two airlines began to circulate as early as 1961. In February, 1964, a Liberal member proposed on the floor of this House that they be merged, with Canadian Pacific holding 50 per cent of the stock in the successor corporation. Considering the relative size of the two airlines at the time, this would have been quite a bargain for CPR shareholders. It is interesting to recall that when the proposal to establish a national airline was first advanced, CPA was offered an opportunity to take part as an equal partner. But it felt the deal was not good enough, and declined to do so. However, once the Canadian people had gone through the agony of building up the airline, the airports and the entire infrastructure required for the operation, CPA became terribly interested. In other words, its attitude

November 25, 1969
Excise Tax Act
was: let the people of Canada take all the risks and we shall come in tor the gravy.
I suggest this type of operation has led to deficits in the operations of our airports-this tendency to let private enterprise take the gravy when it was there to take, while continuing to pick up necessary expenses by using the public purse. In 1965 the Liberal government established spheres of influence for the international services of the two airlines which in effect confined Air Canada to its existing routes in northern Europe and the Caribbean while throwing the rest of the world open to Canadian Pacific. The allocation of the United States market was postponed until after the negotiation of a bilateral agreement with that country, but in 1966 Canadian Pacific was given the route from Vancouver to San Francisco. Whether this was in return for services to the Liberal Party or to the country is not clear from the records.
Also in 1965, Mr. Pickersgill announced that the government would employ a consultant, to advise, and I quote, "whether the growth of domestic main line service would now permit some further degree of competition on that basis and, if so, to recommend a suitable procedure for working out, from time to time, such extensions of service." Mr. Wheatcroft was again hired as the government's consultant, and presented his second report to the minister some time before April 4, 1966. The second Wheatcroft report, unlike the first, has for some reason never been released to the public. According to the Financial Times of April 3, 1967, it found that the establishment of competition on the transcontinental route had neither improved the efficiency of the service nor generated additional traffic. The implication is clear that it recommended against further increases in competition and that it has been kept secret for this reason.
Nevertheless, on March 27, 1967, nearly a year after he admitted receiving the report and five days after Parliament adjourned for the Easter recess, Mr. Pickersgill made a statement of policy concerning the transcontinental airline service: Canadian Pacific would be permitted to increase its service immediately to two daily flights and, beginning in 1969, it would be permitted to occupy 25 per cent of the market. On February 5, 1969, it was announced that Canadian Pacific would be permitted to increase its service to five daily flights in each direction. Since Air
[Mr. Saltsman.j
Canada has only ten flights, this will constitute 33 per cent of the market, rather than 25 per cent. So a series of political decisions has transformed the CPA from a small regional carrier into a major transcontinental and international airline.
Successive governments have deliberately created this situation and justified it with reference to the presumed benefits of competition. If the Liberal government now reverses its stand and eliminates competition by merging the two lines, it will have been party to a scandal unprecedented in our history. In effect, half of the airline owned by the Canadian people will have been turned over to the CPR free of charge, first by gradually allocating routes to Canadian Pacific at Air Canada's expense and then by merging the two on a basis of equality. This can only encourage elements in the business community to make even more outrageous demands. Already an editorial in the Financial Post of January 11, 1969, has demanded that the whole air transport industry be handed over to private interests, with the government completely liquidating its ownership of Air Canada.

speechtext: Order, please. Again I apologize for interrupting the hon. member, but I must say my doubts are stronger now than they were when I first interrupted him. I have been as generous as I can; indeed, I have probably been too generous. I now invite the hon. member to bring his present line of argument to a close, bearing in mind that the rule of relevancy, though often difficult to apply, requires that debate relate directly to what is before the House. At the moment, it is an amendment to the Excise Tax Act which is before use. As I review the explanatory notes, I must say I have difficulty in reconciling the hon. member's argument with the contents of the bill.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I have a few more words which will conclude this portion of my argument. However, I wish to assure Your Honour that when a tax is brought in which will affect every passenger who uses the airline service, it must be considered part of air transportation policy. Although it may in this case fall under the direct responsibility of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), it will have an effect on transportation policy and this is why I
November 25, 1969

have discussed it in a somewhat wider context than usual.
I conclude with these remarks: We in this party will do our utmost to ensure that the Canadian people are not deprived of their national airline through a series of cynical bargains with private interests. We will demand that Air Canada shall not be deprived of the opportunity to prosper and expand while making low-cost transportation available to its real owners, the people of this country. We will resist any fallacious argument which claims that the transfer of this great public resource to private interests is either necessary or desirable. Most of the world's great airlines, outside of the United States, are in public hands. With the support to which they are entitled from their respective governments they can meet the challenge of the supersonic era.
We in this country have suffered too much at the hands of innefficient private enterprise. We have an airline of which we can be enormously proud. Despite all the roadblocks which have been put in the way of Air Canada, it is still one of the great airlines of the world. We in this party cannot see our way clear to vote for this obvious camouflage, this 5 per cent surtax, to cover up the consequences of the inefficient stupidity of the policy followed by the government in connection with air transportation in this country.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief, because as all other members, I should like us to proceed as quickly as possible to the consideration of other government bills, because we have a very full legislative program.
Bill C-155 is no more no less than the levying of a new tax on air travel.
The minister will have, I believe, the opportunity to tell us how much that new tax will bring in and how the government will use the millions thus collected.
I would like to draw the attention of the Minister to the following text: Air travel is the mode of transportation used more and more by businessmen. It is a fast and therefore should be used not only by the inhabitants of big cities, but also by those of the areas that the governments are trying to develop.
Yet, in the region I have the honour to represent, there are problems concerning landing strips and if I were sure that the 21545-8}
Excise Tax Act
amounts the government intends to get through this new tax would be used to enlarge landing strips at municipal airports, it would not be so bad. It would still be a tax, but at least one would know that it would be used to improve difficult situations.
In my opinion the government should answer these questions because as it has examined all aspects of this problem, it should certainly be able to do so.
Nevertheless, the most practical solution is that suggested by the Ralliement creditiste members who always use the same hammer to drive in the same nail. The harder and longer it is, the harder they must strike. If the government thinks that a new tax would be the ideal solution, I repeat that consumers will have less money in their pockets. There will be charges which will very often be added to production costs. So the consumers of goods and services will again have to pay the total cost.
I know that the government needs money for its projects, a few of which though under way are temporarily stopped due to lack of funds. In my opinion it would be to the advantage of the government to study once more the possibility of using the Bank of Canada for this purpose.
This tax revenue the government obtains from consumers originated somewhere, so could not the government discover that new money can also exist in the form of services, instead of debts.
That is why I urge the sponsor of the bill to seriously consider our suggestion. Unless very specific replies as to the use of these funds are forthcoming, I must necessarily oppose this new tax because it is the taxpayers who will be paying the piper, and they are all already complaining about not having enough money.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us an amendment to the Excise Tax Act to authorize an air transportation tax of two kinds, one consisting of a 5 per cent ad valorem, tax for transportation to areas spelled out in the bill-including Canada, the United States, except Hawaii, and St. Pierre and Miquelon-and another tax applied on a straight per capita basis on travel to all offshore areas.
I think the introduction of an amendment of this kind demands that the minister supply the House with justification for imposing such

November 25, 1969
Excise Tax Act
a tax. In this regard I think we in the House are becoming very slipshod. The government states that money must be collected for this, that or the other purpose without justifying the need. I think the members of this House should be told why the imposition of this tax is necessary.
The minister has not revealed the amount of money that is required to be raised, or to what use the money is to be put. I should like to know whether the money will be deposited in the consolidated revenue fund, or into a special trust fund created for the specific purpose of providing funds to meet the cost of construction and maintenance of airports. I would be remiss if I did not remind the House that when the Conservatives were in office several airports were built. For example, we had to meet the bill for four airports, Dorval, Malton, Winnipeg and Edmonton, all beautiful, large airports which were constructed without the necessity of imposing a tax of this kind on the taxpayers of Canada. We on this side of the House support the principle that he who uses should pay. In other words, those who use the airports should pay for their construction and maintenance. I do not think those Canadians who live in isolated parts of Canada and who seldom use airport facilities should be expected to pay for these facilities.
If the principle of taxing those who use the airports is a correct one, how will it be applied? According to this amendment, 5 per cent will be added to the cost of an air ticket. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out that a person who travelled return from, say, Toronto to Ottawa would pay a tax of $2.10, which is 5 per cent of the air fare, whereas a person travelling from Toronto to Vancouver, taxed on the same basis, would pay five or six times as much.
Let us just analyse this situation. A person travelling between two airports, regardless of the length of his journey, occupies the same number of square feet at the airport terminal, uses the same parking space area and requires the same checking facilities and rest rooms, use of restaurant, and so on, as a person who travels the short distance from Ottawa to Toronto. So I think it would be a much fairer assessment if it were on a per head basis across the board. Everybody would then pay the same. The arguments I have put forth for this proposition are, I think, sound and reasonable. The United States have imposed a 5 per cent transportation charge,

and they are not satisfied with it; there is great political pressure to have it changed. One of the greatest arguments against it is put in the form of a question. They ask: Why should the long-haul passenger be subsidizing the short-haul passenger?
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
When the time comes to revise air transportation rates, people will sit down around the table and discuss the situation. They will realize that a passenger on a short trip will be paying only $2.10 in tax. One can visualize their coming to the conclusion that the rate can be increased, but not to the long-distance passenger. I am trying to visualize what might happen when the time comes to make adjustments in the rates.
Nothing was said about whether this tax would apply to air freight or express. Perhaps the minister did say something about that, but I did not hear him. It is apparently left to the Governor in Council, or the cabinet, in respect of overseas charges; they will decide whether the tax is to be $2 or $5. Surely it would be better for us to know now what the rates will be. Let us establish them now so that we are not buying a pig in a bag, as it were. Those are some of the points that come to my mind. I hope there will be a freewheeling discussion during the debate on this subject and that all hon. members will have a chance to take part in it.
Let me quote from the Financial Times of Canada, the November 24 issue, which says in part:
Transport department officials suggest the tax would bring in $20 million in new revenue to the government.
That is a lot of money. At this moment I think we might ask whether, with the invention of the short take-off aircraft which has proven capable of taking off in a fraction of the distance now required, this extra revenue will be needed to cover the cost, or will it more than cover it? We should keep this in mind. The article continues:
This tax would increase income at all airports by almost 50 per cent (currently it is $42 million annually). Conversely, it would make a reasonable dent in the operating losses of the airports. The national accounts figure for 1968-69 placed these at about $58 million.
But apart from doing nothing to cut into the "substantial" expense of maintaining air services- air traffic control and telecommunications networks are two examples-the point about how the money would be used still lingers.
November 25, 1969

That bears out what I was saying when I commenced my remarks. The House should be supplied with more detail as to why this tax is necessary. It is sill right for us to say we need more money, but how will we get it? We are going to again tax the poor taxpayer. Let us put a priority on the taxes we intend to thrust on the taxpayer Is this a priority tax? To conclude my remarks I should like to repeat what I said at the beginning. We need more information about amendments to the Excice Tax Act before we can intelligently vote one way or the other.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak very briefly on this bill. I do so because it is an inequitable and discriminatory measure which should not pass in its present form. The hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out, and most of us agree, that if the money required to operate our airports, derived from fees charged and other revenue obtained from the operation, is not sufficient to meet the cost, it would be more equitable to meet the cost by charging the people who use the airports-in other words, the passengers-than by assessing that cost to the general population and taking it out of the consolidated revenue fund.
As far as a tax is concerned, I think most people would agree that this is the equitable way of paying whatever costs are incurred. However, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Wellington, we do not know how much money is required to meet these costs. We do not know whether the tax proposed will just cover the extra cost, or whether it will bring a greater amount of revenue into the consolidated revenue fund. Before the measure is passed we should have before us the estimates of the Department of Transport and the Department of Finance in respect of what this tax will be used for, and where it is going if it is in excess of the amount really required to meet those airport expenses now borne by the federal government.
The person who travels from Ottawa to Montreal and makes use of those two airports is in exactly the same position, as far as the use of the airport is concerned, as the person who travels from Vancouver to Montreal. I see no reason why the person who travels from Vancouver to Montreal should pay several times as much in the form of taxes for the use he makes of those airports than the person who travels from Ottawa to Montreal.
Excise Tax Act
The tax is discriminatory of people in outlying areas of this country who fly considerable distances to get to the seat of government or the two major cities in this part of the country. A number of people from the east and from the west have to come to Toronto and Montreal for business reasons. This tax is particularly discriminatory so far as people in the city of Calgary are concerned. That city generates a very large amount of air traffic,, much larger than the per capita figure for any other city in Canada. Calgarians travel a great distance to Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto and various places in the United States in connection with the oil business. Therefore, this tax will be particularly burdensome to the citizens of that city. If it is necessary to impose a tax in order to meet airport costs, it should be imposed on a per capita basis; it should not be imposed as is proposed, that is, as a percentage of the total fare. This proposal will result in people living in outlying sections of the country paying more taxes. Let me remind hon. members of the regional development schemes the government proposes for those areas now being discriminated against because of economic and geographical conditions. The proposal before us will impose a further burden on these people. It is a burden they should not be asked to bear. Therefore, I hope this legislation will be modified so that whatever taxes are imposed will be imposed on a straight per capita airport basis, rather than as a percentage of total fare.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps there is no need for my saying anything because most of the points that have been raised-*
Hear, hear.

-have been covered adequately by my eminent colleagues. Looking back at those remarks one sees that several opinions have been expressed in respect of the principle of this type of taxation. Several hon. members have expressed agreement with the proposal, but I have not been convinced.
I want to emphasize one point mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Harkness). It appears to me that this tax will certainly have an adverse effect on people coming from places which are far from the centre of Canada which most people consider to be the Toronto-Montreal complex. People coming from the Atlantic region, for example-if I may be a little parochial-will certainly be overtaxed as a result of the proposed legislation. I cannot stand here with

November 25, 1969
Excise Tax Act
a clear conscience and support a tax which will discriminate against people from my part of Canada. If I were living in Hull, I would agree with this new tax because I would not have to do any flying. But I have to do a fair amount of flying between Gander and St. John's, Newfoundland, and there are in this position hundreds of small businessmen who are trying to make ends meet and who will perhaps go under when the white paper on taxation is enacted into legislation. When this piece of legislation becomes effective they will certainly go under.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Before I can agree to the proposed tax I would like to know what the money will be used for. This is not a complicated question and it is one to which all Canadians want an answer. I have heard that the government plans to spend $6 million in Ste. Scholastique. It plans to renovate the Vancouver Airport facilities to the tune of some $30 million, and I understand a controversy is shaping up, enhanced by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), over airport facilities in the Toronto area. If that is what the money will be collected for, and the government has made these commitments, I as a Canadian taxpayer, my 70,000 constituents and 22 million Canadians would like to know if in fact they are the plans of the government.
Last year I was pressuring a friend of the Premier of Newfoundland, The Minister of Transport, for action on the facilities at the International Airport at Gander We are entering an era wherein 8,900-foot runways are no longer adequate and we need at that airport, as I imagine is needed at most airports in Canada, an extension of the runway facilities to accommodate larger and faster aircraft which need 11,000-foot runways. If these are the sort of things for which this money will be used, then I might change my attitude.
Another question which I would like to raise is the following: We are talking about efficiency. I have been in the House of Commons only a few months and every day I have been hearing about government efficiency. Today I learned that a $400,000 investment of Canadian taxpayers is going into refurnishing the new Department of Communications.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I take the liberty to remind the hon. member that the rule of relevancy has to be taken into account. The hon. member is straying very far from the
[Mr. Saltsman.l
principle of the bill and I ask him to return to the subject matter of the bill before the house. Most certainly if the hon. member is allowed to adopt the line of thinking and argument which he is putting forth to the House at present, other hon. members will want the same privilege, to which they would be entitled. We would then be discussing everything under the sun except what is before the House. I invite the hon. member to keep that in mind.
Hear, hear

Mr. Speaker, I do not understand why members of the NDP are applauding your decision. This is hardly understandable after listening to their speeches. I wanted to establish a point, and not being one of the learned group of lawyers perhaps I am not stating my premises very clearly. I have been trying to establish a connection between efficiency and the government, and the government's need for more taxes. I am trying to put forward the point of view that if I am to support this tax increase, I would like to see more efficiency in government spending.
Hear, hear.

A point of concern to many Canadians is that the Canadian people are perhaps among the highest taxed of the free nations of the world, and this additional taxation will have increasing repercussions. Where will the line be drawn? We are now being taxed directly and indirectly, as economists can confirm, in order to finance airports and so the government can provide a service to the Canadian people. Then we turn around and suggest imposing a tax on the Canadian people for the use of a service for which they have already paid. What tax will we impose for the use of post offices? Shall we increase postage from six cents to eight cents? On looking at the bill before us I come to the conclusion that some of the points raised by hon. members have not been taken into consideration. It seems to me that this bill does not reflect a great deal of thought; as a matter of fact, it appears that it was hastily concocted in order to raise a quick buck. This is my impression.
Questions such as the one raised by the hon. member for Calgary Centre and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) have not been taken into consideration, nor have questions about the effect on a person who uses airport facilities three or four times

Excise Tax Act
November 25, 1989
a week or six or seven times a month, such as the small businessman who makes $8,000 or $10,000 a year and is forced to frequently use these facilities in order to carry on his business. What happens to the man who has to spend a significant proportion of his expense account money on which he will not be able to claim a tax rebate after 1971?
What will happen to air freight? This is a significant question. In Newfoundland we depend to a large extent on freight coming in by air in order to take care of the needs of our people. We bring in products from Ontario and Quebec by air. Are we to be further taxed? What about people who live in places such as Vancouver, the far north and some places in Newfoundland: they will pay a proportionately higher rate relative to their earnings, in comparison with people in other parts of Canada.
What about the per capita increase? If we are going to increase taxes, let us apply the increase equally to all Canadians. What about the users of private aircraft: are they going to have to pay taxes for the use of airport facilities? I am referring to the numerous small companies which operate private businesses with small aircraft. I do not see any reference to these people in the bill before us. What about the administrative costs of administering the $20 million which will be collected? I hope I am not again guilty of skirting the issue, but it seems to me that the administrative cost of such a tax, or of a capital gains tax, is such that the ultimate revenue derived will be negligible.
I will not continue my remarks because I know other hon. members would like to speak. I should like to hear Liberal members, NDP members and other Conservative members who come from other parts of Canada raise questions about the implications of this tax in respect of the people they represent. If the government is in a financial mess, let us face facts and collect taxes directly; let us not impose a tax on a tax, the administrative costs of which would render the ultimate results negligible.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments about this tax as it affects the northern sections of our country. In the years since I came to Ottawa I have come to realize that so far as this government is concerned the development of the north is something to forget about.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Ever since the Liberal government took office back in 1963 it has tended to discourage the development of the north. I say this tax is in keeping with that theme. We had a roads to resources program instituted by a Conservative government. It held out a good deal of hope to the people of the north that they might finally have some of the ordinary amenities that Canadians in other parts of the country enjoy. When the Liberals assumed office, they discontinued that program. Many of the people in the north live in isolated villages scattered many miles apart. Often their only means of communication with the southern regions of the country is by air, and in most cases by chartered air service. As you know, Mr. Speaker, chartered air service costs two or three times, and maybe four times as much as the use of commercial aircraft, but people in northern Alberta, as well as those in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon frequently must use chartered air services because there is nothing else available to them.
A man travelling from Fort Chipewyan to Fort McMurray has the choice of going by dog-team in wintertime, by boat in summertime or by using chartered air service. The first two methods of travel are highly unacceptable. We are here being asked to place a tax burden on people already greatly burdened through having to use chartered aircraft. The minister should pay special attention to this problem. It is a great problem for people who live in the north. I believe he should make an exception in their case, or possibly should forget about this proposed tax so far as people who use chartered aircraft are concerned.

Certainly we all know taxation is like death. There is a certain inevitability about it, an inevitability which under this government is being compounded.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not like to use the word "creeps" which my hon. friend has used; it may be taken out of context. Finally, Mr. Speaker, as I intend to point out when we get into a clause by clause study, there are some rather peculiar clauses in this bill. I am not going to debate them now; I just want to refer to them so that my friends can express themselves: when we get into committee. Clause 14 (1) gives to somebody-I do not
November 25, 1969

know who, but presumably the government- an inordinate amount of power, stating:
14(1) Where an amount is paid or payable outside Canada for the transportation of a person by air
(e) by any other arrangement with a person outside Canada for the benefit or convenience of a person in Canada
Mr. Speaker, that is a very wide, very woolly, very loose clause and the minister might have a look at it when we get to the committee stage. He might well attempt to interpret and explain it, and that is why I am raising it now. As I see it, if I were to travel from Ottawa to New York and then ask someone there to reserve for me a ticket from New York to San Francisco, even though I had paid the tax on my Ottawa-New York ticket it would seem, within the meaning of clause 14, that at the whim of the government I might also be called upon to pay 5 per cent tax on the ticket for the New York-San Francisco and return trip. I think this is a too far-reaching power to trust to any government, and certainly this government.
Mr. Speaker, I would also ask the minister to look at clause 18. We are quite anxious to facilitate the passage of this legislation, tailored to what we think it should be when the changes are made. Clause 18 (d) provides:
The Governor in Council may by regulation ...
(d) determine for the purposes of this Part when transportation begins or ends
(i) at a point in Canada
And so on. This seems to be a rather wide power to give to any government, much less this rather extraordinary government. I hope that the minister will have looked at this question by the time we come to that clause.

Mr. Speaker, as usual I do not stand and merely criticize for the sake of criticizing. I have a positive suggestion to make in this regard. I am afraid this is a rather hasty piece of legislation because of the number of suggestions already made, and because the terms of reference have not been laid down to the satisfaction of members. I should like to make some suggestions on ways to raise revenue as an alternative to this measure.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, when we are building airports I think we should cut down the excessive waste of the taxpayers' money on such frills as modern sculpture. Yesterday in Vancouver Airport I saw three yellow slabs of metal and I did not know what they were. I thought they were snow-scrapers until
Excise Tax Act
somebody told me that it was a piece of modern architecture or sculpture. It cost the people of Canada $150,000-$150,000 for three flat slabs of metal!
Explain.

In Edmonton Airport there are two paintings on the wall. I am not sure of the figures, maybe they are exaggerated, but the story I heard was that these two so-called paintings cost the taxpayers of Canada $26,000. One is a semi-circular piece of wall-board on which somebody has stuck some old burlap. They pasted it on, because there are lumps of paste, ordinary flour and water, as big as your thumb; and three colours, yellow, red and black. I do not know whether that is called art or not. It is not a painting; it is not even decorative. There is another one, blue, white and black, somewhat the size of the end of this building. It is supposed to be another painting. Although I am an art lover and have dabbled a little with paint, I do not think this is an area in which the taxpayers' money should be spent, nor do I think that we should come to them afterwards saying that we want to add 5 per cent to the air fare in order to decorate-and I put that word in italics-the airports of Canada with such poor items of art.
The next question is how to raise the money, as an alternative to this new tax. I would suggest that every airport in Canada might have reasonable entertainment for people held up anywhere from one to twelve hours waiting for airplanes. Why not theatres, slot TV, proper restaurants? It is true that some Canadian airports have good restaurants, but in most of them the eating facilities are precambrian; I think that is the best description. One would fare better by taking along a lunch-box. Generally speaking, the eating facilities in our airports are a disgrace. Why not put in decent theatres, slot machine TV and restaurants? If we had proper facilities at the airports I am quite sure they would make money.
The ground transportation situation at Canadian airports is a standing joke. In bad weather it takes longer to get to Ottawa Airport from downtown than it does to get from the airport to Toronto. Surely with a little co-operation at the three levels of government the capital of Canada could produce one decent road. I know I would not mind paying a considerable sum of money in order to have rapid and comfortable transportation between here and Ottawa Airport. It is something we

November 25, 1869
Excise Tax Act
need, something we are willing to pay for, and the taxpayers' money and my money would be spent in a good cause.
In many cases the ground transportation at airports is a disgrace. I wonder how many people here have complained about having to walk more than a mile at Dorval Airport in Montreal. There are no proper facilities for porters or even hand-carriers to take the luggage. I have seen elderly women lugging great suitcases for a mile, on foot. In little countries like Holland and Belgium the luggage is taken from one plane or train to another for the passenger, without charge. I think my suggestions might earn millions of dollars over the years, so why not provide decent facilities at the airports and in and out of the airports?
A lot of money could be raised by improving the international air facilities to and from Canada. During the past six weeks I have received approximately 100 letters from business firms and private individuals all over Alberta requesting that the major airlines serving the United States, Alaska and abroad be allowed to enter the international airport at Edmonton. I was astounded to learn that our great airports refuse this sort of service. In the twentieth century why should we be denied the right to travel to any airport in the world if we are willing to pay the price? The argument as to whether one should pay a per capita charge, as provided in this piece of legislation, or whether it should be as a percentage of the ticket is one I have not resolved myself. I should like to have more information in this regard.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
At present the situation appears to me to be most unfair. A traveller flying long distances will have his overhead increased by a considerable percentage as a result of this unfair tax. I think this question might well be looked into. Perhaps a compromise could be worked out. The government may wish to introduce a combination of a percentage of the ticket price plus a toll. Instead of the flat 5 per cent, there might be a toll plus, say, a tax of $2 for the use of the airport. A small percentage could be charged, so that the man travelling long distances would not be paying less, proportionately, than others using the airport. Instead of merely saying, "Let us put a 5 per cent tax on, through which we will raise 'X' dollars," the government ought to be looking for ways to apply a measure like this more equitably. As I say, there might be a toll

plus a percentage, in terms of money, of the distance the ticket will take a traveller.
It would be wise if we did not tax too heavily those people from other countries who use Canadian airports. The tourist industry, which is the second largest industry in Canada in terms of net revenue, brings in vital foreign exchange. We want tourists from all over the world to come here, enjoy our mountains and outdoor facilities when on holiday and leave with us their very much needed dollar and sterling currencies with which to balance our payments.
Being interested in the development of the north, I have taken a realistic look at this matter. It would be shortsighted on our part to bring in a tax which would slow down the pace of mineral and oil resource discoveries in newly explored areas of the Northwest Territories and the Arctic islands. It would be particularly shortsighted if the government were to hamper that part of our industry which is racing United States industry in an effort to explore and develop our Arctic coastline in the shortest period of time and with the least possible overhead.

Mr. Speaker, without doubt Bill C-155 is one of the most inequitable pieces of legislation this government has brought in. I cannot too strongly criticize the government's attitude in bringing forward this bill. Many people in our country want to travel, and this tax will make it more expensive for them to do so. This, therefore, is a wrong tax to bring in at this period in our history. The Standing Committee on Transport and Communications went to Labrador and Newfoundland in September. We found, during the course of our trip, that people in the Schefferville, Wabush and Labrador areas will have to pay exhorbi-tant air fares if they wish to travel. That being so, for heaven's sake let us stand up and be counted in our opposition to this measure.
Is the government really concerned about this nation? By imposing this sort of tax the government is being most unfair. The bill shows clearly that those who are travelling farthest will have to pay most. Has the government no consideration for those in this country who must live on fixed incomes? By introducing this measure the government has shown, again, that it has no compassion for those who must live on fixed incomes and who may wish to travel overseas or elsewhere. Even those wishing to go by charter flights must pay. I hope the minister will
November 25. 1969

clarify this point when he sums up. Those who have managed to scrape up enough money to go by charter flight will have to pay this extra cost. Possibly they will not find it in their power to go on those tours we have all been hearing about.
Many of our people wish to travel, but this tax may make it impossible. Clearly, those who travelled to Harrison Hot Springs last week-end were not worried about the 5 per cent tax. They could afford to go. They do not fall into the category of those who are least able to pay higher transportation costs. As I said, many thousands of our people would like to travel, but this new type of tax will add to their expenses in the future and will limit their travelling.
The transportation systems of this country need overhauling and we need a comprehensive transportation policy. Even though we have a Transport Commission and the National Transportation Act on the statute books, the government has adopted a piecemeal approach to transportation, as is evidenced in Bill C-155. If the government were really concerned about providing transportation for the people of this country, it would not have adopted this piecemeal approach. Let us have a complete and comprehensive transportation policy that will allow everyone in this country to travel, and not just those who have affluent positions in our affluent society.
Many applications have been held before the Canadian Transport Commission on the subject of abandonment of railway passenger services. In my opinion the board should not automatically grant such requests. The board should consider over-all transport policy. It seems evident, nevertheless, that the government is not really concerned about introducing such a policy for Canada which will be applicable from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Now that the "Bullet" is no longer in service in Newfoundland, the people of that area have to rely more on air transport. The government is now asking them to pay an additional 5 per cent for their air tickets if they want to travel by air in Canada or to other parts. It is disgraceful that the government should tell the people of this country that if they want to travel by air they must pay an extra 5 per cent for their air tickets because extra airport facilities are needed. I hope the government will carefully reconsider the 5 per cent tax to be imposed after Bill C-155 has received passage.

Everyone in this country who is not now directly affected by this measure may ultimately be affected by it. Surely the advent of the new jumbo jet will remove the need for this tax. Jumbo jets will be able to carry many people. If members of the government are looking ahead-and it seems that at Harrison Hot Springs they were able only to look ahead and not to examine the present-to 1971, 1972 and 1973, they will see that jumbo jets may provide an answer to this problem. In the meantime, let us all realize that 5 per cent extra on an air ticket is a major item for many people of this country who are still earning less than $30 a week.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the minister speaks now he will close the debate.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, as is usual in these circumstances, I think hon. members expect me to attempt to respond to at least some of the points that they have made.
The hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales) suggested that not enough details had been presented by me with respect to this tax and its purposes. In my opening statement I did attempt to say something about the purpose of the tax. I said and I quote, "As explained by the Minister of Finance at that time",-I was referring to the June 3 budget speech-"the cost of construction and maintenance of air transportation facilities is very high and, in addition to obtaining revenue from user charges at airports, the government has decided that it is advisable to ask Parliament to require individuals who travel by air to pay an amount through what in effect will be a special tax to help defray the costs of providing air transportation facilities".
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I might have used the opportunity given to me in the opening of the second reading debate to have said even more. I felt, however, that hon. members would not have wanted me to take the time of the House for this purpose in view of the rather complete explanation of the purpose of the tax given by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), when he presented his budget statement on June 3, 1969. Perhaps I might at this point summarize some of the things the Minister of Finance said during the budget statement because I think it will help answer the quite legitimate request of the

November 25, 1969
Excise Tax Act
hon. member for Wellington for details about the purpose of the tax, the revenues expected and so on.
In the budget statement the Minister of Finance said that a further measure of budgetary significance arises out of a general policy to ask those who benefit directly from a service or facility provided by the government to pay charges more in line with the direct costs involved. Several speakers from the official opposition seemed to accept this principle and support it, although in fairness to them I think I should note that they felt that the tax on flights within North America should be added on a flat rate basis rather than ad valorem. I will attempt to deal with this argument later in my remarks.
The Minister of Finance went on to say there would be a review of user charges and in addition the introduction of some new charges. He said, as reported at page 9420 of Hansard:
In almost all cases this action can be taken under existing legislation. There is one important field, however, where legislation will be required to impose what will in effect be a tax. This relates to air transport.
It is well known that our expenditures on the construction, equipment, operation and maintenance of airports and other air transport facilities are now very large. In the last fiscal year they are estimated at $73 million. The revenue we obtain from user charges, rents, etc. of one kind and another related to airports and air transport facilities is far less-only about $41 million-
The minister went on to say:
We have decided, however, on one measure which we believe should be enacted by parliament as soon as possible to assist in providing more revenue in this field.
He continued:
We propose that a charge, tax, be levied on the price of tickets or other charges (such as charter hire) made by air carriers for carrying passengers in or from Canada on trips commencing with a date to be specified in the legislation. We have worked out a tentative plan for such charges which we believe would yield revenues of about $20 million a year.
I assumed most hon. members were familiar with the information provided by the Minister of Finance in his budget statement. I felt they would not have wanted me to repeat them in my opening statement, although I am very happy to do so to help make the record on this debate more complete. The hon. member for Wellington asked where the proceeds of the tax will go. I understand the proceeds will go into the consolidated revenue fund. Generally speaking, the amount raised will be taken into account in determining the

amount that the Department of Transport will be spending on air transport facilities.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), accepting as he did the general principle that users of facilities should bear an appropriate proportion of their cost, argued that the tax should be a flat tax rather than an ad valorem tax. It is true that the bill does not attempt to make the amount of tax depend directly or precisely upon the use of an airport or the use of navigational aids. This is something that would be very difficult to do. It should be stressed that this is not a tax simply for the use of an airport or airports. As I understand the proposed tax, it is to help provide revenues to pay for the use, maintenance and expansion of the air transport facilities generally which are provided by the federal Department of Transport.
I gather this would include the facilities of air navigation, air traffic control, meteorological and so on, not simply the use of the airport structure itself. If I am correct in this, it seems that some of the arguments put forward by hon. members who have spoken to the effect that the tax is not fair because there are some people who will use an airport once and others will use it three times, are not as valid as they would be if the tax were to be used solely for bearing the cost of maintaining the airport structure itself, something which I am informed is not the case. The tax in effect is imposed on the amount paid for transportation. This is basically analogous to the manner in which sales taxes and excise taxes are imposed. As I said in my opening remarks, this is a tax upon consumption. In other words, as I understand the sales tax it is basically a percentage of the price of the goods purchased.
Don't you know?

I believe the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) suggested that what is done by somebody travelling by car is quite different from the proposed tax. He suggested there is a flat amount paid, I suppose for the licence or registration of the car, and there is another tax paid which is linked with the amount of gasoline that the person uses to travel about in his car. He suggested the proposed excise tax is something different. Perhaps I am wrong in this, but it seems basically that it is quite similar.
If a person travels from Vancouver to Ottawa he uses more gas; it costs him more money since he pays a greater amount of tax
November 25, 1969

on that gas. This seems to be analogous to what is involved in somebody travelling from Vancouver to Ottawa by airplane rather than by car. It costs more than travelling by airplane from Toronto to Ottawa and therefore the tax to that equivalent extent would be greater, just as it costs more by way of tax on gasoline to travel by car between Vancouver and Ottawa than to travel by car between Toronto and Ottawa.
Although I thought the hon. member was putting forward an interesting argument, I felt, and perhaps I am incorrect, that it tended to support the argument for an ad valorem tax rather than the argument against it. If a flat tax were imposed upon every trip by air within Canada and to points in North America, the amount of such tax would probably have to be $5. This would result in a tax equal to about half the fare for persons flying on short trips such as from Fredericton to Saint John, New Brunswick or from Vancouver to Victoria. Some people would end up paying a 50 per cent tax if the proposal put forward by some hon. members of the official opposition were accepted rather than the 5 per cent ad valorem tax proposed by the government.
Hon. members should note it is likely that a flat tax per trip within the taxation area as defined in the bill before us would create many complications. For example, if the tax were imposed on each trip, it would apply on both legs of a return trip ticket. It would be very difficult and probably impossible to fairly define a return trip ticket. For example, would a trip from Ottawa to Winnipeg and back from Winnipeg to Ottawa via Toronto be a round trip ticket? Would it be a round trip ticket if the passenger came back from Winnipeg to Montreal instead of to Ottawa?
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
If the tax applied to each purchase of a ticket, passengers would include in one purchase all the transportation they might require for a couple of months and then transfer the unused portions. This would add seriously to the cost for the airlines and to the cost of auditing.
If there were to be a flat rate tax imposed on each trip, I presume hon. members would be arguing for a tax which would be in the form of a departure tax collected each time a passenger boarded an aircraft. I suggest such a tax would greatly add to the paperwork at airports and would seriously slow down the flow of passengers through terminals. As the
Excise Tax Act
hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Bigg) remarked, delays at airports due to congestion, and so on, are already serious enough and the imposition of a departure tax would certainly add to the congestion-it would become even worse as the jumbo jets embarked even larger numbers of passengers all at the same time.
A flat departure tax would contain a number of elements of unfairness. For example, if there were such a tax, a passenger flying from Toronto to Vancouver who is unable to get a through flight but who has to stop at Winnipeg and Edmonton uses four airports and logically, I suppose, could pay four departure taxes. But why should he pay more tax than the person who flies directly from Toronto to Vancouver? Then again, a tax payable every time an airport was used would cause passengers to seek a through service and thus might help one airline at the expense of another.
There are other points which should be noted. One argument against the advisability of a flat rate tax of the type proposed by the hon. member is that to produce the same total revenue there would certainly have to be a substantial increase in the tax on short distance travel, and this might have the effect of distorting the demand for short distance air travel in a way which would create competitive problems vis-a-vis other modes of transport.
I have already suggested that this tax is intended to yield revenue to provide services for air travellers, services which are not confined to landing and take-off. Indeed, aircraft have access to a much more comprehensive range of services which are used throughout the flight, from the point of take-off to the point of landing.
I might point out, also, that the United States already imposes a 5 per cent ad valorem tax. As I said in my opening remarks, taxes in connection with air travel have international ramifications. Our major airlines in Canada, Air Canada, Canadian Pacific and so on, are international carriers and are already geared administratively to collecting the United States ad valorem tax.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) suggested that this tax would place an unfair burden on the airlines when it came to collect them. The system proposed is generally that which is used at the present time for the collection of sales tax, a similar form of tax, and our major carriers are already collecting such a tax at the present

November 25, 1969
Excise Tax Act
time on flights in the United States which attract the United States ad valorem tax.
The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Salts-man) began by saying that the proposed tax is not businesslike and that it represents, in effect, a subsidy to business. However, the hon. member for Edmonton West said the tax would impose an unfair burden on business. Well, both these hon. gentlemen cannot be right. It would appear that as usual the proposal of the government strikes a fair balance between these two extremes in a way which is not adverse to the interest of any segment of Canadian society.
One or two hon. members referred to the impact of this tax on charter flights and suggested it would make things difficult for people who had saved up for many years to take such flights. I would point out that most of the charter flights of which I am aware go to overseas points and, as I indicated earlier, flights to overseas points would attract not an ad valorem tax but a flat tax which, if applicable, would be calculated on the basis of the number of seats in the aircraft. I believe I mentioned that the flat tax would initially be at the rate of $5 for each ticket sold, with authority being given to the Governor in Council, if Parliament agrees, to reduce this to a lower amount. The reason Parliament is being asked to give the Governor in Council authority to reduce the tax is that at the present time the United States does not impose a tax on overseas flights although there is a bill pending before Congress which would not only increase the ad valorem tax from 5 per cent to 8 per cent but would create a flat tax on overseas flights in an amount of approximately $3.
Obviously, if the United States Congress passes a bill along the lines I have outlined it will be necessary for Canada to make appropriate adjustments in the tax on overseas flights from Canada, otherwise passengers will be encouraged to purchase tickets in the United States rather than in Canada.
I return to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Waterloo in case there is some misunderstanding on this point. Contrary to what he has suggested, the proposed tax would not go to pay for the running of Air Canada; the proceeds would be used, rather, for maintaining airports and air transportation facilities and to assist in defraying the cost of there expansion which is presently being carried out by the Department of Transport.

While the hon. member made some interesting comments about national airline policy, the question of whether it is desirable to have one, two, or more airlines which are national in scope is not really before us at this time. I might add, however, without passing judgment on what the policy should be, that it is my understanding that since Canadian Pacific is a private firm it does pay taxes to the federal government, probably at the top corporate rate of 50 per cent. So to the extent it makes profits the federal government and the federal taxpayer generally share in them to the extent of 50 per cent. It would seem to me that the growth of air traffic will require the expansion of air transportation facilities no matter how many airlines national in scope we possess. Whether there is one, two or three, the traffic generated will have to be handled.

The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) has asked for information on the revenue this new tax would bring in. As I have mentioned earlier, I believe this will be around $20 million.
The same member has also asked to explain the purpose of this new tax. If we look once again at the budget speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on Tuesday, June 3, 1969, we find that the minister said, and 1 quote:
A further measure of budgetary significance arises out of a general policy to ask those who benefit directly from services or facilities provided by the government to pay charges more in line with the direct costs involved.
Speaking about costs, he said, and I quote:
-our expenditures on the construction, equipment, operation and maintenance of airports and other air transport facilities are now very large.
It is with these aims in mind that I am asking the support of the House to levy this new tax.
The hon. member spoke in a very interesting manner of using the Bank of Canada to grant the necessary credits.
It is indeed on interesting possibility but I suggest that it is not the time, when we are discussing the budgetary resolutions adopted on June 3 to amend the present financial policy. I am sure that we shall have other opportunities to discuss the rather interesting financial policy of the Ralliement creditiste.
November 25, 1969

[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)

Might I also try to clear up a couple of other points raised by hon. members. I thought it was clear from my explanatory remarks-I regret if it was not-that my understanding was that this tax will not be imposed on air freight. Neither will the tax be imposed on charter flights on aircraft with a load less than 18,000 pounds. Other categories of flights are also not subject to the tax, but I will give further details during the committee of the whole stage.
These exceptions will, I think, effectively answer many of the points made by hon. members who expressed concern about the possible impact of the tax on those living in isolated areas. Such exemptions from the impact of the tax will remove many of the fears hon. members seem to have. I would be happy to attempt to answer in greater detail some of the more specific points raised by hon. members,, in due course. However, at this time the House might be willing to give its support to the bill on second reading.
