speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am most happy that my fellow citizen from Vancouver has brought this matter before the House. We find there are in greater Vancouver today some 6,000 federal civil servants. We have been assessing the requirement for them to be in the centre of the city. We have decided that because of the interests of the public in certain departments, about 2,400 would be required to be in the very busy centre core of the city.
We have decided that the balance, including a number in laboratories and the like, could be located in less dense areas where transportation might be better and where the land values are not so high. As my hon. friend knows, that particular area bounded by Granville Street, Hastings Street, Howe Street and Cordova Street contains probably the highest priced land in the city of Vancouver. We are at the present time working on a preliminary study of the requirements for a federal building in Vancouver. I know my friend will be glad to hear that.
At the present time these people are housed in eight old federal buildings in Vancouver, and 21 leased buildings. My hon. friend might agree with me, as most Vancouver members will, that some of the accommodation there is of a type that means the morale and efficiency of civil servants cannot be of the best. We are therefore proceeding as rapidly as possible and I intend to make an announcement fairly soon.
My hon. friend referred to Project 200. Because of the critical area in which we are located, making it necessary to obtain clear access from Granville Street and Howe street, it is our intention to keep everyone apprised of what we are doing co-operatively in respect of proper access levels. We want to be a good landlord within the centre of the city, and therefore have over a period of years had discussions with the mayor, city councillors and planners. The mayor and his councillor have indicated to us that they would prefer us to go on the east side of Granville Street for a variety of reasons which my hon. friend can appreciate. It is our intention to continue these discussions and to co-operate with Vancouver in every respect.
I think this is about all I have to say on the subject at present. We will proceed as rapidly as we can. I want to make the point that not only in Vancouver but in other parts of Canada it is imperative that the national government have a national presence, and I

NATIONAL REVENUE-DELAY IN FEDERAL SALES TAX AUDITS OF COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 19, I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) the following question:
In view of the fact that federal sales auditors have not made annual inspections or audits of many Canadian companies, for up to as long as four or five years, and that in many cases when they do these audits they reassess the companies for thousands of dollars in taxes, what steps is the minister taking to overcome this problem and to make sure that there will be more frequent and regular inspections?
This question was not acceptable at the time, so in the few minutes that are available to me tonight I should like to put forth the following problems. The reason for the question was that I have received several letters from small and large companies which have not had government sales tax auditors on their premises for as long as four or five years. I have had two specific cases brought to my attention, one of a small company which had not seen a federal auditor for four years and seven months, following which they were presented with a bill for $3,419.95 which was due for sales which had been exempted from tax in error. You might say this relates only to small companies, but that is not so. Another very large company, which had not seen a government sales tax auditor for four years, was presented with a bill for $80,000. This amount is not peanuts; it is a very large bill to present to any company, large or small, particularly when they cannot go back and bill their customers. I know the minister will probably say that owing to the austerity program there is not sufficient manpower to make these audits more frequently; but one of these cases occurred three or four years ago, before the austerity program was put into force.
The problem is accentuated by the fact that the department does not send out notices or information to companies in a clear and legible way. They send them out, but do not use plain, ordinary English or plain, ordinary French, whatever the case may be, so that the operators of the companies can understand the regulations and keep their books according to the wishes of the department. I do not think there is any doubt that the inspections
DEBATES	1247
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion should be made more frequently. I realize that the companies are responsible for collecting these taxes, but in many cases there are very difficult decisions to be made, namely is it taxable or is it not.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I know the Department of National Revenue re-organized their whole set up a few years ago. They decentralized. This was in order to give better service. But from talking to my constituents I have found the experience has been that the service is not as good as it used to be.
I do not like to criticize the department without offering some constructive criticism. I think it is high time the government started to collect all tax moneys through one department and had one auditor make the complete audit of a business firm or taxpayer. Why should a man in business have to get out all his books for the sales tax collector, and then a few months or a year afterwards have another inspector arrive from the Income Tax Department and he has to bring out all his books again? The unemployment insurance auditor is the third fellow who comes around, and then we have the Canada Pension Plan auditor coming on the scene as well.
Why could we not have one auditor from the Department of National Revenue to audit all the books on one trip and thus cut down on the cost of the operation? It is very difficult for a man in business to produce invoices that go back four or five years, yet he has to dig up all these invoices. It is a tremendous job and a costly one, and it is only necessary because the government does not conduct audits with the frequency to which a man in business, be he large or small, is entitled.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Public Works):
maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-DELAY IN FEDERAL SALES TAX AUDITS OF COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire, on behalf of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote), to give this answer. In reply to the question raised by the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales) concerning the possibility of conducting audits for sales tax purposes more frequently than is now the practice, the following are some of the factors which inhibit any change in our present policy in this area.
At the present time we have some 58,000 persons or firms licensed under the Excise Tax Act and experience has shown that the average time expended in conducting an audit of a licensee's records is 2.15 days. Our staff of operational auditors across Canada numbers approximately 265. Apart from the difficulties of acquiring and training staff
1248	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion there is the necessity to see that those employed are applying themselves to those accounts which are most complex because of the variety and volume of their output.
The risk to the revenue by reason of faulty application of the law is of course greater than in other more simple operations. On this basis we therefore use the manpower resources available to us to the greatest advantage, for we have programmed our audits on the basis of a two, three and four year cycle depending on the complexity of the operation involved and the past assessment history of the licensee concerned, which we have found to have worked quite well.
Every step, of course, is taken to help the taxpayer. Our auditors meet with new licensees at the earliest moment after they have started in business. This is usually around the sixth month of their operations. They are then assisted in solving any tax problems they have or may foresee. A check is made to see that they are receiving all the published information issued by the department for their guidance, and they are invited to communicate with our officials at any time they might have any questions to ask. With our regional set-up, more expertise is available to them within shorter distances. On the average we conduct the greater part of our audits within 24 to 30 months.
The only way in which we could meet the suggestion of the hon. member as to annual audits be conducted, would be by more than doubling the number of auditors in our work force. This would be contrary to government policy and we are convinced that it would not be justified on a cost-benefit basis as our experience has shown that approximately 54 per cent of the audits conducted result in no assessment whatever. If we were to attempt to conduct audits every year with our present audit staff, I feel certain that the examination would be a hit-and-miss affair and accordingly not very meaningful in the light of established priorities.
I would like to assure the hon. member that we are working continually to improve our audit program in order to provide the best service possible consistent with the limits of our financial and manpower resources. I might further explain that there is no statutory provision requiring us to audit a licensee's record at any stated interval, and by the same token there is no authority in the Excise Tax Act whereby retroactive assessments may be waived. None the less, our continual objective is to keep retroactive assessments at a minimum.

maintopic: VIOLENT DISTURBANCES-MONTREAL- BOMBING AT LOYOLA COLLEGE-INCREASED CO-OPERATION BY R.C.M.P.
VIOLENT DISTURBANCES-MONTREAL- BOMBING AT LOYOLA COLLEGE-INCREASED CO-OPERATION BY R.C.M.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday, November 21, I asked the Acting Prime Minister if he would contact the Mayor of Montreal and the Premier of Quebec to inquire if anything more could be done by the federal government, including the R.C.M.P., to prevent further terrorist bombings in Montreal. My question followed the bombing at Loyola College on Thursday, November 20, when a powerful bomb exploded in a classroom building while 400 evening students were in class.
The same week in Montreal a bomb was placed in the home of the Deputy Mayor of St. Michel. These were only the most recent of a long series of bombings in Montreal. Since I did not get any real commitment for action at that time, I decided to raise the question for debate at the time of adjournment.
While the citizens of Montreal have been seriously concerned for some time, the incident last Thursday gave them new cause for alarm. A few weeks previous to the bombing, Michel Chartrand, a union leader in Montreal, told a public meeting that if Quebec Bill 63 should become law there would be a new wave of violence in Quebec. Bill 63 passed on Thursday evening and the bomb at Loyola exploded the same night. While there may be no connection between the statement by Mr. Chartrand and the bombing at Loyola, the innocent public of Montreal wonder whether there will be more bombs and whether their lives and the lives of their children are in danger. If the students at Loyola last Thursday had been in the corridor when the bomb went off, scores of them would have been killed. Luckily, they were all in their classrooms at the time.
Mr. Speaker, I am not an alarmist, but with many others in Montreal I am beginning to wonder whether we have to wait until innocent people are killed before the efforts of the police forces at all levels are intensified. Even though Mr. Chartrand is not directly connected with the bombing at Loyola, are we to tolerate a society where leaders in the community can make threats of violence with apparent impunity and thereby encourage terrorism? I hope that people who are not satisfied with Bill 63, among other things, in Quebec realize that violence is counter-production and in the long run will destroy everything.

November 25, 19G9

In tonight's Star there is an article which says that Lucien Saulnier, the chairman of the executive committee, will be in Ottawa later this week and that one of the subjects he may take up with the federal government is a request for assistance for Montreal police in their battle against terrorism. The article says in part:
A request for assistance for Montreal police in their fight against terrorism in the city could be made in Ottawa later this week by Executive Committee Chairman Lucien Saulnier.
The executive committee is curently reviewing the role of the municipal police in combating terrorist activity. Members are understood to feel that the city police should not have to bear the brunt of the battle and that the city should not have to pick up the entire tab.
Then it states:
The co-operation of the R.C.M.P. and the Quebec Provincial Police with the municipal police in fighting the different groups of terrorists active in the city...is of doubtful benefit in the minds of many senior officers.
Off the record, officers of all three forces will admit that the "co-operation" is far from "total and complete".
Mr. Speaker, without criticizing any one officer, because probably a lot of the men in the police forces are working very hard on this matter, I say without criticism of what has been done that we must intensify our efforts to prevent and deter further bombings and also to discover those persons responsible for the bombings that have already taken place. I hope the government at the federal level will do everything possible to assist the provincial and municipal governments in this task, and I hope I will get a commitment to that effect from the minister and the government.

maintopic: VIOLENT DISTURBANCES-MONTREAL- BOMBING AT LOYOLA COLLEGE-INCREASED CO-OPERATION BY R.C.M.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share, as I am sure all hon. members do, the concern of the hon. member
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion about the bombings and related acts of violence taking place in a wholly abnormal way in the city of Montreal. However, the facts are that the federal police force authority and those responsible for it are co-operating fully with the municipal and provincial police forces. This co-operation is not an academic exercise; it is worked out in a carefully organized way among the police forces having the responsibility for dealing with this matter. Mr. Speaker, I thought I gave that assurance last Friday when the question was asked and I went on to say:
-I want to emphasize very strongly that there is very close working co-operation between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Quebec Provincial Police and the city of Montreal police in these matters, and in this particular instance there is. of course, that kind of co-operation.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I was referring to the Loyola incident. It is quite true that the initial or prime responsibility lies with the local authorities; but in addition to offering co-operation we have offered every assistance possible. I know of no request for any assistance that has not been granted, and I know of no way of bringing additional assistance, at the moment. We will continue to co-operate fully with the respective authorities in trying to deal with this problem and, in addition, give them all the assistance we can. That is the way the matter stands.
As to the report in the newspaper tonight- I assume the hon. member was referring to the Montreal Star and not to the Toronto Star-I can only say that I have not seen that report and do not wish to comment on it. It was written by a reporter and may or may not be correct in any detail. I shall look at the article and see if anything in it warrants attention, but I would prefer not to comment specifically on it in an offhand way.
